A fern with a long history in European folk medicine, where it was once believed to heal snakebites and ward off evil spirits. It's less commonly eaten in Nepal, but its medicinal reputation has traveled across the globe—an ointment made from it was used for wounds and ulcers, a practice that continues in some rural communities.
identification: A small fern with a single, simple leaf blade and a separate spore-bearing stalk. The plant grows 5–20 cm tall. The whole plant is sometimes used.
habitat: Grows in temperate regions, often in grasslands, meadows, and open woodlands. Found in Europe, Asia, and North America.
fun_facts: Grows 5–20 cm tall. Found in temperate regions worldwide. Used in European folk medicine for centuries. Contains compounds with medicinal properties.
trivia: In medieval Europe, adder's tongue was believed to be an effective remedy for snake bites, leading to its common name. The plant was also used as a charm against evil spirits. Large quantities can cause severe health problems.

description: This fern has traveled far from its origins, becoming a popular vegetable in Indonesia and a medicine in the Philippines. Its young fronds are gathered and eaten, a practice that connects Nepali foragers with islanders thousands of miles away—a shared knowledge of wild food that spans continents.
identification: A small fern with a single, simple leaf blade and a separate spore-bearing stalk. The plant grows 10–25 cm tall. The young fronds are the edible portion.
habitat: Grows in tropical and subtropical regions, often in grasslands, open forests, and disturbed areas.
fun_facts: Grows 10–25 cm tall. Found in tropical and subtropical regions. Popular vegetable in Indonesia. Used in traditional medicine in the Philippines.
trivia: This fern is sometimes called the 'net-veined adder's tongue' because of the distinctive network of veins visible on its leaf blade. In Indonesia, it's an appreciated vegetable sold in local markets.

trivia: Air potato is a prolific climber and is considered an invasive weed in some regions, but its tubers are a valuable food source in many parts of Asia.

trivia: In Nepal, ajwain is often added to pickles and spice blends for its distinctive flavor.

Almonds are grown in Nepal's mid-hills, though not on a large scale. The nuts are prized for their flavor and health benefits. The tree is a deciduous species that blossoms in early spring with pinkish-white flowers.
identification: A deciduous tree reaching 5–10 m with oval, serrated leaves. The fruit is a drupe with a hard shell containing the edible almond kernel.
habitat: Grows in temperate climates with dry, hot summers. Found in orchards in the mid-hills.
fun_facts: Grows 5–10 m tall. The kernel is the edible part. Rich in healthy fats. Grown in Nepal.
trivia: Almonds are native to the Middle East. In Nepal, they are often eaten as a snack or used in sweets. The tree is also grown for its ornamental value.

fruit_type: Drupe (with a hard shell containing edible seed)

description: The nut that's gaining popularity in Nepal's hills—almonds are a nutritious nut, rich in vitamin E and healthy fats. The trees are grown in the mid- and high-hills.
fun_facts: Almonds are native to Central Asia.
They are rich in vitamin E and healthy fats.
The fruit is eaten as a nut.
trivia: In Nepal, almonds are often eaten as a snack or used in traditional desserts.

culinary_uses: Leaves cooked as sag, dried and stored
medicinal_uses: Rich in iron, calcium, and vitamins A and C
description: A nutritious leafy vegetable that's widely consumed in Nepal. Amaranth greens (latte ko sag) are rich in iron and calcium, making them a healthy addition to the diet. The leaves are cooked as sag.
fun_facts: Amaranth greens are more nutritious than spinach in some respects.
They are rich in iron, calcium, and vitamins.
The leaves can be dried and stored for use during the lean season.
trivia: In Nepal, amaranth greens are often dried to make gundruk, a fermented green that's a staple in hill households.

uses: Fresh, pickles, candied, Ayurvedic remedies, hair oil, Chyawanprash, juice, murabbah, curries
description: A small, sour fruit packed with more vitamin C than an orange. Amla is an Ayurvedic superfruit, revered in traditional medicine for thousands of years for its health-promoting properties. While its taste may pucker your mouth, its benefits are legendary. In India, Nepal, and Sri Lanka, amla is a cornerstone of traditional wellness.
identification: A small to medium-sized deciduous tree reaching 8–18 m with feathery, compound leaves. The fruit is round, 2–3 cm in diameter, with smooth, greenish-yellow skin and fibrous, sour, pale green flesh. It contains a small, hard seed.
habitat: Grows in tropical and subtropical climates. Found in forests, gardens, and along field edges in the Terai and mid-hills. Prefers well-drained soil and full sun.
fun_facts: Grows 8–18 m tall. Fruits are 2–3 cm in diameter. Contains 300–600 mg of vitamin C per 100 g. A key ingredient in Ayurvedic medicine. Amla is native to India and Sri Lanka.
trivia: Amla is known as the 'Indian Gooseberry' and is one of the main ingredients in Chyawanprash, a traditional Ayurvedic tonic. In Nepal, it's a common sight in markets during winter. In Sri Lanka, amla is used in traditional remedies for hair health.

description: The crisp, sweet fruit of the high hills—apple is a temperate fruit that thrives in Nepal's high-altitude regions. The orchards of Jumla and Mustang produce some of the finest apples in the country.
fun_facts: Apples are native to Central Asia.
Nepal's apples are known for their crisp texture and sweet flavor.
The fruit is rich in antioxidants.
trivia: In Nepal, apples are often eaten fresh or used to make juice and jam.

description: A hardy stone fruit that thrives where few other fruits can. Apricots are the golden jewels of the trans-Himalayas, sun-dried on rooftops and cherished through long mountain winters. In Mustang, dried apricots are a vital food source and export. From Turkey to California, apricots are prized for their sweet, delicate flavor.
identification: A deciduous tree reaching 5–10 m with rounded, toothed leaves and white to pink blossoms. The fruit is small, round to oval, 3–5 cm in diameter, with smooth, golden-yellow skin and sweet flesh surrounding a single large seed.
habitat: Thrives in dry, temperate and trans-Himalayan climates. Found in high-altitude valleys of Mustang, Manang, and Dolpa. Prefers well-drained, sandy soil and full sun.
fun_facts: Grows 5–10 m tall. Fruits are 3–5 cm in diameter. Thrives at altitudes up to 4,000 m. Essential for nutrition in high-altitude regions. Turkey is the world's largest apricot producer.
trivia: In Mustang, apricots are sun-dried on rooftops during late summer. The dried fruits are a vital winter food and are exported to lower-altitude markets. In Armenia, the apricot is considered the national fruit.

A plant with a deadly beauty—its flowers are hooded and striking, but its tubers are packed with irritating crystals. The young shoots are eaten after careful processing, a skill that has been passed down through generations. In Nepal, it's a wild plant that demands respect and careful handling.
identification: A herbaceous plant with a distinctive hooded flower spathe. The young shoots are the edible portion after processing.

fun_facts: Found in the Himalayas. Has toxic tubers. Harvested in April-May. Has distinctive hooded flowers.
trivia: The tubers of Arisaema species contain calcium oxalate crystals, which are highly irritating to the mouth and throat. The young shoots must be thoroughly cooked or processed before eating. In Nepal, it's a wild food that requires careful preparation.

They must be cooked, a lesson that has been passed down through generations. In East Asia, it's a valued vegetable; in Nepal, it's a lesser-known treasure of the wetlands.

fun_facts: Found in temperate and subtropical regions. Tubers can be eaten like potatoes. Harvested in July-August. Used in traditional medicine.
trivia: The tubers of this plant are called 'kudzu' in Japanese and are used as a vegetable in East Asian cuisine. The plant was also used by Native Americans as a food source. In Japan, arrowhead is a traditional New Year's vegetable.

A wild edible fruit found in Palpa district, Nepal. It's likely a relative of jackfruit or breadfruit, but little is known about its local uses. It's one of the many under-documented wild fruits in Nepal.
identification: A tree with large, lobed leaves and a fruit similar to jackfruit but smaller.
habitat: Found in forests in Palpa district.
fun_facts: Found in Palpa district. Related to jackfruit.
trivia: This species is part of the rich biodiversity of Nepal's lower hills. More research is needed to document its uses.

description: Another wild fig-like fruit from Palpa district, likely the lakoocha or monkey jack. Its fruits are edible and sometimes used in local cuisine. It's a lesser-known relative of the jackfruit.
identification: A tree with large leaves and a fruit that resembles a small jackfruit, with orange-yellow flesh.
habitat: Found in forests in Palpa district.
fun_facts: Related to jackfruit. Found in Palpa district.
trivia: The lakoocha fruit is sometimes eaten fresh or cooked. Its wood is also used for timber.

uses: Fruit eaten as vegetable and offered to gods during festivals
description: A large, pale green gourd that is both a vegetable and a religious offering. In Nepal, ash gourd is cooked in curries and also used in festivals. Its flesh is mild and absorbs flavors well.
identification: A climbing vine with large, lobed leaves and yellow flowers. The fruit is large, oblong, 20–40 cm long, with a waxy, pale green skin and white, watery flesh.
habitat: Grows in tropical and subtropical climates. Cultivated in gardens and fields.
fun_facts: A climbing vine. Fruits are large, 20–40 cm long. Used as a vegetable. Used in religious offerings.
trivia: Ash gourd is also known as winter melon. In Nepal, it's often used in the festival of Bhai Tika. The fruit can be stored for months without spoiling.

description: A local variety of Asian pear, named after Pharping near Kathmandu. It's a unique genetic resource, used for making jams, juice, and wine. Its fruits are crisp and juicy, with a slightly grainy texture.
identification: A deciduous tree with oval, glossy leaves and round, yellow-brown fruits with a grainy texture.
habitat: Grown in orchards in the mid-hills, particularly around Pharping.
fun_facts: A local variety. Used for jam, juice, wine. Found in Pharping.
trivia: The Pharping local pear is a unique variety that is being conserved for its genetic value. It's a popular ingredient for homemade wine in the Kathmandu Valley.

description: A creeping vine with triangular leaves and small, blue-black fruits. In Nepal, the fruits are edible and sometimes used in local cuisine. It's a plant that colonizes open, disturbed areas.
identification: An annual, trailing vine with triangular leaves and small, blue-black fruits.
habitat: Grows in open, disturbed areas in the hilly region.
fun_facts: A trailing vine. Fruits are edible. Found in hilly region.
trivia: This plant is also known as 'mile-a-minute' due to its rapid growth. In Nepal, it's sometimes used as a green manure.

description: A climbing asparagus with edible shoots and medicinal tubers. In Ayurveda, it's known as shatavari, a female tonic. In Nepal, the young shoots are eaten as a vegetable, and the tubers are used in traditional medicine.
identification: A climbing plant with feathery leaves and tuberous roots. The young shoots are the edible portion.
fun_facts: Young shoots edible. Tubers used in Ayurveda. Known as shatavari.
trivia: Asparagus racemosus is a well-known medicinal plant, used to support reproductive health in women. In Nepal, it's a valuable wild vegetable.

description: A weed with medicinal uses, asthma weed is used for skin ailments and as an antidote for snake bites. In Nepal, it's called dudheghans and is used in traditional medicine.
identification: A small, hairy herb with opposite leaves and tiny, green flowers.
habitat: Tropical and subtropical regions, in disturbed areas.
fun_facts: Used for skin ailments. Antidote for snake bites. Common weed.
trivia: Euphorbia hirta is widely used in traditional medicine for respiratory and skin conditions.

Avocado is a newcomer to Nepal's mid-hills, but it's gaining popularity for its creamy, nutritious flesh. It's often eaten fresh, in salads, or as guacamole. The tree is subtropical and does well in the warmer hills.
identification: A medium-sized evergreen tree reaching 10–15 m with large, glossy leaves. The fruit is pear-shaped, 10–20 cm long, with a rough, green to black skin and creamy, yellow-green flesh containing a single large seed.
habitat: Grows in subtropical climates. Found in orchards in the mid-hills.
fun_facts: Grows 10–15 m tall. Fruits are 10–20 cm long. Rich in healthy fats. A recent introduction to Nepal.
trivia: Avocados are native to Central America. In Nepal, they are often eaten with salt and pepper or used in smoothies. The fruit is also a good source of potassium.

uses: Fresh, sharbat, laxative, squash, richest source of riboflavin
description: The hard-shelled aromatic fruit that holds a sacred place in Hindu worship. Offerings to Lord Shiva always include bel leaves—they are said to please him. The fruit's dry fibrous pulp, when mixed with water and sugar, becomes a cooling summer drink that is both a remedy and a treat. It's a fruit that feeds both body and soul.
identification: A medium-sized deciduous tree reaching 6–12 m with thorny branches and aromatic leaves. The fruit is round to oval, 5–10 cm in diameter, with a hard, woody shell that turns yellow-green when ripe. Inside is a dry, fibrous pulp with numerous hairy seeds.
habitat: Grows in tropical and subtropical climates. Found in Terai gardens, orchards, and sacred groves. Prefers well-drained, sandy soil and full sun.
fun_facts: Grows 6–12 m tall. Fruits are 5–10 cm in diameter. Rich in riboflavin. Used in Ayurvedic medicine for digestive issues. The leaves are sacred to Lord Shiva.
trivia: In Nepal, bael is often planted near temples. The unripe fruit is used in curries, while the ripe fruit is made into a refreshing sherbet. In India, the fruit is celebrated in folk traditions.

description: A giant bamboo whose young shoots are used as a vegetable. In Nepal, it's called bans. It's used for jaundice.
identification: A tall, clumping bamboo with thick, woody culms.
fun_facts: Shoots edible. Used for jaundice. Popular vegetable.
trivia: Bamboo shoots are a staple food in many Asian cuisines. They are crisp and nutritious.

season: Year-round with peaks in winter and summer
uses: Fresh, cooked, fritters, desserts, religious offerings, banana blossom as vegetable
description: A constant companion through every season—there's always a bunch ripening in the kitchen corner, ready to be eaten fresh, fried into golden fritters, or offered to the gods. The plant is a giant herb masquerading as a tree, its 'trunk' just layers of leaves wrapped tight. From the highlands of Rwanda to the plantations of Ecuador, this humble fruit feeds millions daily.
identification: A tall herbaceous plant growing 3–8 m with large, paddle-shaped leaves up to 2 m long. Fruits grow in hanging clusters (hands) of 10–20 bananas. Fruits are elongated and curved, yellow when ripe, with creamy white flesh.
habitat: Thrives in tropical and subtropical climates. Found in home gardens, orchards, and field edges. Prefers well-drained, fertile soil and full sun.
fun_facts: Grows 3–8 m tall. A single bunch weighs 20–50 kg. Ready to harvest in 9–12 months. One of the most widely consumed fruits globally—over 100 billion bananas are eaten worldwide each year.
trivia: Banana plants are herbs—the 'trunk' is a pseudostem of tightly packed leaves. In Nepal, banana blossom curry (kera ko bungo) is a delicacy. In Uganda, bananas are a staple food eaten with almost every meal.

description: A wild banana species, rich in vitamin C and minerals. In Nepal, it's also called bankera.
identification: A large herb with a pseudostem and edible fruits.
fun_facts: Fruits edible. Rich in vitamin C. Has antioxidant properties.
trivia: Wild bananas are ancestors of the cultivated banana and have many seeds.

culinary_uses: Fresh, cooked (plantain), in desserts
medicinal_uses: Rich in potassium; good for heart health
cultural_significance: Used in religious ceremonies (offerings)
economic_importance: Important fruit and food crop
description: The versatile fruit that's a staple in Nepal's Terai—banana is eaten fresh, cooked, and used in desserts. The tall banana plants sway in the Terai breeze, and the fruit is an essential part of Nepali cuisine and culture.
fun_facts: Bananas are technically berries.
Nepal produces many varieties of banana, including cooking bananas (plantains).
The fruit is rich in potassium and other minerals.
trivia: In Nepal, bananas are often offered to gods during religious ceremonies.

An evergreen shrub with spiny branches and bright yellow flowers—chutro is a familiar sight in Nepal's hills. Its small, red berries are edible, with a tart flavor that is used in drinks and traditional remedies. The plant is also valued for its medicinal properties, especially for treating fever and inflammation.

habitat: Grows in temperate forests, forest edges, and scrublands at elevations of 500–1,500 m. Found in the mid-hills.
fun_facts: Grows 1–3 m tall. Fruits are 5–10 mm in diameter. Rich in vitamin C and alkaloids. Used in traditional medicine. Related to the European barberry.
trivia: In Nepal, chutro berries are often made into a refreshing drink or wine. The plant is also used in traditional remedies for high blood pressure and diabetes. In Europe, barberry was once used as a condiment.

medicinal_uses: Barley water for digestive health
unique_characters: Grows up to 4,000 m; extremely cold-tolerant

description: The hardy survivor—barley grows where the air is thin and the winters are harsh. It's the cereal of the high Himalayas, cultivated in the cold deserts of Mustang and Dolpa.
fun_facts: Barley is one of the oldest cultivated cereals, with evidence dating back to 10,000 BC.
In Nepal, it's grown up to 4,000 m, making it one of the highest-altitude cereals in the world.
It is also used as animal feed and for malting in the brewing industry.
trivia: In Nepal's high Himalayas, barley is often roasted and ground into flour to make tsampa, a staple food of Tibetan communities.

culinary_uses: Cooked as porridge
medicinal_uses: Gluten-free; good for diabetics
unique_characters: Quick-maturing; good for short growing seasons
description: A quick-maturing millet that provides food for hill communities. Barnyard millet is a hardy crop that can grow in poor soils and is valued for its nutritional content.
fun_facts: Barnyard millet is also known as 'Japanese millet'.
It matures quickly, making it suitable for areas with short growing seasons.
It's gluten-free and rich in fiber.
trivia: Barnyard millet is often grown as a catch crop after the main rice harvest.

culinary_uses: Dried leaves used as spice in curries and dals
medicinal_uses: Good for digestion; rich in antioxidants
cultural_significance: Used in traditional medicine and rituals
description: The fragrant leaf that's essential in Nepali cooking—bay leaf (tej pat) is used as a spice in curries and dals. The tree is native to the Himalayas and grows in Nepal's mid-hills.
fun_facts: Bay leaf is native to the Himalayas.
It's used as a spice in South Asian cooking.
The leaves have a distinctive, fragrant aroma.
trivia: In Nepal, bay leaves are often added to curries and rice dishes for their aroma.

description: A plant with edible leaves, found in the Himalayas. Related to the lily.
identification: A herb with broad leaves and blue-black berries.
fun_facts: Leaves edible. Found in the Himalayas.
trivia: Clintonia species are often grown in shade gardens for their attractive berries.

description: A deep red root vegetable that's gaining popularity in Nepal. Beetroot is eaten boiled, roasted, or in salads, and is rich in iron and folate. The leaves are also edible.
fun_facts: Beetroot is rich in iron and folate.
Both the root and the leaves are edible.
It's a cool-weather crop.
trivia: In Nepal, beetroot is often used in salads and as a juice. In Eastern Europe, beetroot is a key ingredient in borscht.

A common grass whose shoots are used in traditional medicine for cuts and wounds. In Nepal, it's called dubo.

habitat: Tropical and subtropical regions, in disturbed areas.
fun_facts: Used for wounds. Considered good for health.
trivia: Bermuda grass is a common lawn grass and also has medicinal uses.

description: A bitter, edible fruit used as a vegetable. In Nepal, it's called tite karela and is valued for its anti-diabetic properties. It's a staple in many Asian cuisines.
identification: A climbing vine with deeply lobed leaves and warty, elongated fruits that are green and bitter.
fun_facts: Fruits edible but bitter. Used for diabetes. Has medicinal properties.
trivia: Bitter gourd is known for its blood sugar-lowering properties and is widely used in traditional medicine. It's an acquired taste but highly nutritious.

description: A black-skinned pulse that's a staple in Nepali cuisine. Black gram is used to make dal and is also ground into batter for snacks like dhokla. It's a nitrogen-fixing crop that improves soil fertility.
fun_facts: Black gram is native to South Asia and has been cultivated for thousands of years.
It's rich in protein, iron, and other minerals.
The crop improves soil fertility by fixing nitrogen.
trivia: In South India, black gram is the main ingredient in dosa and idli batters.

description: A black raspberry species found in Nepal, known as kaulo binin ainselu. Its ripe fruits are eaten raw, with a sweet-tart flavor similar to other raspberries. It's a wild plant that grows in the hills.
identification: A thorny shrub with compound leaves and black, aggregate fruits.
habitat: Grows in temperate forests and scrublands.
fun_facts: A thorny shrub. Fruits are black and eaten raw. Found in Nepal. Harvested in April-May.
trivia: This wild raspberry is a source of vitamins and antioxidants. It's often foraged by locals and used in homemade wines and jams.

description: A plant whose leaves are used as a vegetable after cooking. In Nepal, it's called kalobihi. It has antiseptic and diuretic properties.
identification: A small herb with black berries and small, white flowers.
habitat: Tropical and subtropical regions, in disturbed areas.
fun_facts: Leaves edible after cooking. Used as a diuretic. Has antiseptic properties.
trivia: Black nightshade leaves are edible when cooked and are used in many cuisines. The ripe berries are also edible.

description: An underutilized walnut species found in Nepal's mid-hills. It's similar to the black walnut of North America, with a strong flavor and hard shell. Its nuts are used for oil and wood.
identification: A large deciduous tree reaching 20–30 m with compound leaves and round, hard-shelled nuts.
habitat: Grows in temperate forests in the mid-hills.
fun_facts: Grows 20–30 m tall. Nuts are hard-shelled. Used for oil and wood.
trivia: In Nepal, this walnut is not as common as the English walnut, but it's a valuable timber species. The nuts have a distinctive flavor and are sometimes used in baking.

description: A plant whose leaves are used as a vegetable. Its juice is used to check bleeding. In Nepal, it's a common weed with edible and medicinal uses.
identification: A herb with opposite, toothed leaves and yellow flowers with black seeds.
habitat: Tropical and subtropical regions, in disturbed areas.
fun_facts: Leaves edible. Juice used to stop bleeding. Found in Nepal.
trivia: Blackjack is a common weed in many parts of the world and is often used as a vegetable in Asia and Africa.

description: Kafal is a wild favorite in the mid-hills—a small, reddish-purple berry that marks the arrival of summer. The trees are dioecious, and only the female ones bear fruit. The berries have a sweet-tart flavor and a large seed. Children often gather them in the forests, their fingers stained with the dark juice. It's a taste of childhood for many Nepalis.
identification: A medium-sized evergreen tree reaching 8–12 m with leathery, serrated leaves. The fruit is a small, round berry, 1–2 cm in diameter, reddish-purple when ripe, with a sweet, tangy pulp surrounding a large seed.
habitat: Grows in temperate forests, often on slopes and along streams in the mid-hills. Prefers well-drained, acidic soil.
fun_facts: Grows 8–12 m tall. Fruits are 1–2 cm in diameter. Only female trees bear fruit. Rich in antioxidants. A popular wild fruit in Nepal.
trivia: Kafal is often sold in local markets during the summer. It is also used to make wine and chutneys. The tree's bark has medicinal properties and is used in traditional remedies.

description: A fern found across the globe, bracken has fed humans since prehistoric times. But here's the warning: it contains poisonous compounds that can cause cancer. Despite this, some cultures still eat it as a delicacy, usually after careful processing. In Nepal, most elders know to avoid it—wisdom that has saved many from illness.
identification: A large, coarse fern with broad, triangular fronds growing up to 2.5 m tall. The plant spreads aggressively through underground rhizomes. The young shoots (fiddleheads) are the edible portion.
habitat: Grows in a wide range of habitats, including forests, grasslands, heaths, and disturbed areas. Found on all continents except Antarctica.
fun_facts: Fronds can grow up to 2.5 m tall. Contains carcinogenic compounds. One of the most widely distributed ferns in the world. Can live for over 100 years.
trivia: Bracken is one of the oldest plants on Earth, with fossils dating back over 55 million years. It is considered a serious weed in many parts of the world due to its aggressive growth. In Japan, bracken is eaten as 'warabi' after careful preparation.

description: A creeping herb used in Ayurveda for cognitive enhancement. In Nepal, it's called khole sag and its shoots are used as a vegetable. It's used for dysentery and nervous disorders.
identification: A small, creeping herb with succulent leaves and small white flowers.
habitat: Wet areas in tropical and subtropical regions.
fun_facts: Shoots edible. Used for cognitive enhancement. Known as brahmi.
trivia: Brahmi is a well-known memory-enhancing herb in Ayurveda, used for centuries.

An aquatic plant with edible shoots, used as a vegetable. Its pollen is also edible.
identification: Similar to T. angustifolia but with broader leaves.
fun_facts: Shoots edible. Pollen used as flour. Found in water.
trivia: Cattail pollen can be used as a flour substitute and is rich in protein.

culinary_uses: Steamed, stir-fried, curried
medicinal_uses: Rich in vitamins C and K, folate, and antioxidants
description: A nutritious green vegetable that's gaining popularity in Nepal—broccoli is a cool-season crop that thrives in the hills. The green heads are used in curries, stir-fries, and salads.
fun_facts: Broccoli is a relative of cabbage and cauliflower.
It's one of the most nutritious vegetables, rich in vitamins and antioxidants.
It grows best in cool weather.
trivia: In Nepal, broccoli is often stir-fried with spices or used in curries.

description: A plant whose leaves are used as a vegetable. It's an appetizer and diuretic. In Nepal, it's called khole sag.
identification: A creeping, succulent herb with opposite, fleshy leaves and small blue flowers.
fun_facts: Leaves edible. Used as an appetizer.
trivia: Brooklime is often found near streams and is used as a wild salad green.

Pers. अज흤बरी Ajambari (Nepali). Perennial herb, entirely glabrous, with stout erect stem to 1.5 m. Petioles 1–7.5 cm, with broadened base. A plant whose leaves are used as a vegetable. Buckwheat is a pseudo-cereal, and its leaves are edible. In Nepal, it's called mithe phapher and is used for constipation and hypertension.
identification: A fast-growing annual with heart-shaped leaves and clusters of white flowers.
habitat: Cultivated in temperate and subtropical regions.
fun_facts: Leaves edible. Used for hypertension. Has medicinal properties.
trivia: Buckwheat is not a true cereal but is used in a similar way. Its grains are gluten-free and nutritious.

culinary_uses: Ground into flour for pancakes, noodles, porridge
medicinal_uses: Good for diabetes; gluten-free
total_landraces: 19 landraces of common buckwheat; 37 for Tartary buckwheat
unique_characters: Gluten-free; matures in just 70-90 days
cultural_significance: Important in high-altitude communities; used in religious offerings
description: The gluten-free hero of the Himalayas—buckwheat is not a true cereal, but it's treated like one in Nepal's hills. It grows quickly in poor soils and cool climates, providing a reliable harvest when other crops fail.
fun_facts: Buckwheat is not a grass and is not related to wheat—it's a relative of rhubarb.
It grows quickly, maturing in just 70-90 days, making it an ideal crop for short growing seasons.
In Nepal, it's often planted as a secondary crop after the main cereal harvest.
trivia: In Nepal, buckwheat is often the only crop that can survive in the high-altitude valleys of Mustang and Manang.

culinary_uses: Ground into flour; often mixed with common buckwheat
medicinal_uses: Rich in rutin; good for cardiovascular health
unique_characters: More cold-tolerant than common buckwheat; bitter taste (tite = bitter)
description: The bitter cousin of common buckwheat—tite phapar grows at even higher altitudes, where the air is thin and the growing season is short. Its grains are smaller and have a slightly bitter taste, but it's a vital crop for communities in the high Himalayas.
fun_facts: Tartary buckwheat is more cold-tolerant than common buckwheat.
It has 37 landraces documented in Nepal.
It's rich in rutin, a flavonoid with antioxidant and cardiovascular benefits.
trivia: Tartary buckwheat is also known as 'bitter buckwheat' (tite phapar) in Nepali.

description: A tropical fruit with a knobby, heart-shaped appearance—bullock's heart, or ramphal, is a relative of the custard apple. Its creamy flesh is sweet and aromatic, with a flavor that reminds you of a combination of banana and pineapple. In Nepal's mid-hills, it's less common but still a treasure where it grows.
identification: An erect shrub or small tree reaching 2–3 m with a spiny stem. The fruit is round to heart-shaped, 8–12 cm in diameter, with a rough, greenish-brown skin and creamy, sweet flesh containing many seeds.
habitat: Grows in tropical and subtropical climates. Found in home gardens and orchards in the mid-hills. Prefers well-drained soil and full sun.
fun_facts: Grows 2–3 m tall. Fruits are 8–12 cm in diameter. Flowering occurs in March-April. Rich in vitamin C and fiber. Native to Central America but now grown in the tropics.
trivia: In Nepal, ramphal is often eaten fresh when fully ripe. In the Caribbean, the fruit is used in drinks and desserts. The seeds are not edible and are toxic.

description: A tree whose flowers and fruits are used as a vegetable. In Nepal, it's called mahuwa. Its flowers are used in respiratory infections, and fruits for chronic ulcers.
identification: A large tree with thick, leathery leaves and clusters of creamy-white flowers.
fun_facts: Flowers and fruits edible. Used for respiratory infections. Rich in nutrition.
trivia: Mahua flowers are used to make a sweet, alcoholic drink in many parts of India and Nepal.

culinary_uses: Fresh in salads, cooked in curries, fermented
medicinal_uses: Rich in vitamin C and K; good for digestion
description: The round, leafy vegetable that's a staple in Nepali winter kitchens—cabbage is used in curries, salads, and pickles. It's a cool-season crop that thrives in the hills, and it can be stored for months.
fun_facts: Cabbage is one of the oldest vegetables, with cultivation dating back to 4,000 years.
It's a cool-season crop that grows best in the hills.
Fermented cabbage (gundruk) is a traditional Nepali food.
trivia: In Nepal, cabbage is often fermented to make gundruk, a tangy, fermented vegetable that's a staple in many hill households.

description: The caper plant is famous for its pickled flower buds. In Nepal, its shoots and fruits are also edible. It has hepatoprotective properties and is used in traditional liver tonics.
identification: A spiny, trailing shrub with round, fleshy leaves and large, white flowers.
habitat: Dry, rocky areas in subtropical and tropical regions.
fun_facts: Flower buds pickled. Shoots and fruits edible. Used in liver tonics.
trivia: Capers are a staple in Mediterranean cuisine. The plant is well-adapted to arid environments.

description: The jewel of Nepal's eastern hills—large cardamom (bariyo alamchi) is a high-value spice that grows under the shade of forest trees. Nepal is one of the world's largest producers of large cardamom.
fun_facts: Large cardamom is native to the eastern Himalayas.
Nepal is one of the world's largest producers of large cardamom.
It's a high-value cash crop that supports many hill farmers.
trivia: In Nepal, large cardamom is used in traditional medicine and as a spice in curries and teas.

soil_type: Well-drained, acidic, rich in organic matter
culinary_uses: Used in spice blends, sweets, and teas
medicinal_uses: Good for digestion; used in traditional medicine
unique_characters: Small seeds with a sweet, aromatic flavor
description: The queen of spices—small cardamom (sano alamchi) is prized for its sweet, aromatic flavor. It's used in sweet dishes, spice blends, and tea. Nepal produces some of the finest small cardamom in the world.
fun_facts: Small cardamom is often called the 'queen of spices'.
It's native to India and is grown in Nepal's eastern hills.
It's used in a wide variety of dishes, from sweets to savory dishes.
trivia: In Nepal, cardamom is often added to masala chai, the traditional spiced tea.

description: A crunchy, orange root vegetable that's a winter favorite in Nepal. Carrots are eaten fresh in salads, cooked in curries, and made into a refreshing juice. They're rich in beta-carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A.
fun_facts: Carrots were originally purple and yellow, not orange.
They are rich in beta-carotene, which is good for eye health.
They are a cool-weather crop, grown in winter.
trivia: In Nepal, carrots are often eaten raw as a snack. In Europe, carrots are a classic ingredient in soups and stews.

culinary_uses: Boiled, fried, made into flour and tapioca
medicinal_uses: Rich in carbohydrates
unique_characters: Contains cyanogenic glycosides (must be properly processed)
description: A tropical root crop grown for its starchy roots. Cassava is a minor crop in Nepal, grown mainly in the western Terai. It must be properly processed to remove toxins.
fun_facts: Cassava is the third-largest source of carbohydrates in the tropics.
It contains cyanogenic glycosides that must be removed by cooking.
It's a drought-tolerant crop.
trivia: Cassava is a major staple in Africa, South America, and parts of Asia.

culinary_uses: Not for food (toxic)
medicinal_uses: Oil used as purgative (with caution)
unique_characters: Contains toxic ricin; industrial oil
description: A fast-growing shrub grown for its oil-rich seeds. Castor oil is used in industry, and the plant is also grown as an ornamental. The seeds contain toxic ricin and are not for food.
fun_facts: Castor oil is used in industry for lubricants and paints.
The seeds contain ricin, a potent toxin.
It's drought-tolerant and grows in poor soils.
trivia: In Nepal, castor is often grown as a hedge plant.

description: The beautiful white vegetable that graces Nepali tables—cauliflower is a winter vegetable par excellence. The tight, white curd is used in curries, pickles, and salads. It's a cool-season crop that thrives in the hills.
fun_facts: The 'curd' of cauliflower is actually a cluster of undeveloped flower buds.
It's a cool-season crop that grows best in the hills.
Nepal has many local varieties adapted to different altitudes.
trivia: In Nepal, cauliflower is often used in pickles (kauli ko achar) and as a vegetable in curries.

A plant whose leaves are used as a vegetable after cooking to destroy toxins. It's used for asthma and arthritis.
identification: A herb with glabrous, lobed leaves and small, yellow flowers.
habitat: Wet areas in temperate and subtropical regions.
fun_facts: Leaves edible after cooking. Used for asthma. Toxic when fresh.
trivia: This plant is toxic when fresh but edible after cooking, like many wild greens.

description: A humble creeping herb that is anything but ordinary—centella is known around the world for its brain-boosting properties. In Ayurveda, it's called brahmi and used as a tonic for memory. In Nepal, it grows wild in moist places, and its leaves are eaten in salads or as a vegetable—a green that sharpens the mind while nourishing the body.
identification: A small, creeping herb with round, kidney-shaped leaves on long stalks. The shoots and leaves are the edible portions.
habitat: Grows in tropical and subtropical regions, often in moist, shaded areas, along streams, and in rice paddies.
fun_facts: Found in tropical regions. Used as a brain tonic. Well-known medicinal plant. Harvested from February to April.
trivia: Centella is known as 'Brahmi' in Ayurvedic medicine and has been used for thousands of years to improve memory and cognitive function. It is also used in traditional Chinese medicine. In Nepal, it's a common wild green in wetland areas.

description: In Sri Lanka, they call it mayurkutea—'peacock's umbrella'—for the graceful shape of its fronds. In Nepal, it's a less common fern, but it shares the same medicinal reputation: a remedy for fevers and headaches, a plant that brings relief in the same way in two different lands.
identification: A small fern with dark green, divided fronds. The young fronds are the edible portion. The plant has a short, creeping rhizome.
habitat: Grows in tropical forests, often in moist, shaded areas. Found in Asia.
fun_facts: Found in Asia. Used in traditional Chinese medicine. Harvested in March-April. Eaten raw or cooked.
trivia: This fern is sometimes called the 'peacock fern' due to the shape of its fronds. In Sri Lanka, it is known as 'mayurkutea,' which means 'peacock's umbrella.' In traditional Chinese medicine, it's used to treat fever, headache, and dizziness.

culinary_uses: Cooked as dal; ground into flour (besan) for batters and sweets
medicinal_uses: Rich in protein and fiber
unique_characters: Rich in protein and fiber; nitrogen-fixing
description: A versatile pulse that's a key ingredient in Nepali cuisine. Chickpeas are used to make dal, flour (besan), and snacks. They're a good source of protein and fiber, and are often grown in rotation with wheat and rice.
fun_facts: Chickpeas are one of the earliest cultivated pulses, dating back to 7,500 BC.
They are rich in protein, fiber, and minerals.
Besan (chickpea flour) is a staple in Nepali and Indian cooking.
trivia: In Nepal, chickpeas are often used in snacks like pakauda (fritters) and sekuwa.

description: A common weed with edible leaves, used as a vegetable. In traditional medicine, it's used for asthma, blood diseases, and inflammation. In Nepal, it's known as armalejhar.
identification: A small, creeping herb with oval leaves and small white flowers.
habitat: Temperate regions worldwide, in gardens and disturbed areas.
fun_facts: Leaves edible. Used for asthma and inflammation.
trivia: Chickweed is often used in salads and as a green vegetable. It's also a popular remedy in herbal medicine.

culinary_uses: Fresh in cooking, dried as spice, pickled
medicinal_uses: Rich in vitamin C; capsaicin for pain relief
unique_characters: Contains capsaicin (the heat compound)
cultural_significance: Essential spice in Nepali cuisine
description: The fire of Nepali cuisine—chili peppers are an essential spice that adds heat to curries, chutneys, and pickles. From the tiny, fiery Jire Khursani to the long, mild Dalle, Nepal has a wide variety of chilies.
fun_facts: Chili peppers originated in the Americas and spread to Asia through trade.
The heat comes from capsaicin, which is a natural pain reliever.
Nepal's Jire Khursani is known for its intense heat and fruity flavor.
trivia: In Nepal, chilies are often sun-dried and stored for year-round use. Spicy chili pickle (khursani ko achar) is a favorite accompaniment to meals.

description: A fern that grows across Asia and Australia, with young fronds that are gathered and cooked as vegetables in many communities. In Nepal, it's one of the lesser-known edible ferns, but in neighboring countries, it's a common sight in wild vegetable markets.
identification: A medium-sized fern with dark green, divided fronds. The young fronds are the edible portion. The plant has a short, creeping rhizome.
habitat: Grows in tropical and subtropical forests, often in moist, shaded areas. Found in Asia and Australia.
fun_facts: Found in Asia and Australia. Used in traditional medicine for skin diseases. Related to the brake fern family. Found in tropical and subtropical regions.
trivia: The genus Pteris includes many species that are used as ornamentals in gardens around the world. This species is sometimes called the 'two-eared brake fern.' In Australia, similar ferns are gathered by indigenous communities.

description: A cultivated amaranth with leaves that glow in shades of green, red, and yellow—as beautiful as it is nutritious. In China, it's known as 'yin choy,' a common stir-fry ingredient. In Nepal, it's less commonly grown, but its vibrant leaves are beginning to find their way into market gardens.
identification: An annual herb reaching 0.5–1 m with broad, colorful leaves in shades of green, red, and yellow. The young leaves and shoots are the edible portion.
habitat: Cultivated in tropical and subtropical regions. Grown in gardens and fields.
fun_facts: Grows 0.5–1 m tall. Leaves come in multiple colors. Rich in vitamins and minerals. Cultivated as a vegetable.
trivia: The colorful leaves of this amaranth make it popular not only as a vegetable but also as an ornamental plant. In China, it's known as 'yin choy' and is commonly used in stir-fries. In Nepal, it's gaining popularity as a nutritious leafy green.

Bimero is the oldest citrus fruit—it's been cultivated for millennia. It has a thick rind and little pulp, but its fragrant peel is used in cooking and traditional rituals. In Nepal, it's found in the mid-hills, where it's valued for its aroma and medicinal uses.
identification: A small evergreen tree reaching 3–5 m with large, oval leaves. The fruit is oval to oblong, 8–15 cm long, with a thick, yellow rind and acidic, seedy flesh.
habitat: Grows in subtropical climates, often in home gardens and orchards in the mid-hills.
fun_facts: Grows 3–5 m tall. Fruits are 8–15 cm long. One of the oldest cultivated citrus fruits. Used for its fragrant peel. Rich in vitamin C.
trivia: In Nepal, citron is often used in religious ceremonies and as a natural air freshener. The peel is candied in many cultures and used as a flavoring.

A tree whose fruits are used as a vegetable. In Nepal, it's called dumri and is used for diarrhea and constipation.
identification: A tree with large, ovate leaves and clusters of figs on the trunk.
fun_facts: Fruits edible. Used for diarrhea and constipation.
trivia: This fig is also known as the 'cluster fig' and is a common sight along riverbanks.

description: A fruit so versatile it's called the 'tree of life.' Coconuts provide food, water, oil, and material for daily life. In Nepal's Terai, they are grown in warm pockets and are a staple of religious and cultural ceremonies. From the beaches of the Maldives to the farms of the Philippines, coconuts sustain millions of lives.
identification: A tall, single-stemmed palm reaching 15–30 m with a crown of large, feathery leaves. The fruit is a large drupe, weighing 1–3 kg, with a thick, fibrous outer husk and a hard, brown shell containing coconut water and white kernel.
habitat: Thrives in tropical coastal and riverine climates. Found in Terai gardens and river plains. Prefers well-drained, sandy soil and full sun.
fun_facts: Grows 15–30 m tall. Fruits weigh 1–3 kg. The 'tree of life' provides food, water, and materials. One tree produces 50–100 fruits per year. Coconuts are found in over 90 countries worldwide.
trivia: Coconuts float and can drift on ocean currents, spreading naturally to new islands. In Nepal, coconuts are often used in religious ceremonies and offerings. In the Philippines, every part of the coconut tree is used for food, shelter, and crafts.

culinary_uses: Roasted, ground, and brewed as coffee
medicinal_uses: Rich in antioxidants; good for mental alertness
economic_importance: Growing cash crop in the mid-hills
description: The aromatic bean that's waking up Nepal—coffee is an emerging cash crop in the mid-hills. The high-altitude coffee grown in Nepal has a unique, rich flavor that's gaining recognition in international markets.
fun_facts: Coffee is the second most traded commodity in the world after oil.
Nepal's coffee is known for its distinct flavor profile.
The crop was introduced to Nepal in the 1930s.
trivia: In Nepal, coffee is often served black or with milk.

description: A plant with edible leaves, related to Solomon's seal. In Nepal, it's used as a tonic and to heal wounds. Its leaves are used as a vegetable.
identification: A herbaceous plant with arching stems and oval leaves.
fun_facts: Leaves edible. Used as a tonic.
trivia: The coiling leaf gets its name from the tendrils at the tip of its leaves, which coil around supports.

culinary_uses: Green pods as vegetable; dry seeds as dal
medicinal_uses: Rich in protein and fiber

description: One of the most versatile legumes—common beans are grown as both a vegetable (green pods) and a pulse (dry seeds). In Nepal's hills, many local landraces of beans are cultivated, each adapted to its own microclimate.
fun_facts: Common beans are native to the Americas and were domesticated over 7,000 years ago.
They are a good source of protein, fiber, and minerals.
Nepal has many local landraces, including two registered varieties: Khairo and Pahenlo Simi from Dolakha.

description: The aromatic green that adds life to Nepali dishes—coriander (dhaniya) is an essential spice. The fresh leaves are used as a garnish, while the dried seeds are a key ingredient in spice blends. It's the heart of Nepali flavor.
fun_facts: Coriander is one of the oldest spices, with cultivation dating back to 5,000 BC.
Both the leaves and seeds are used in cooking.
The seeds have a different flavor from the leaves.
trivia: In Nepal, coriander chutney (dhaniya ko achar) is a popular condiment, made with fresh coriander leaves, chili, and lemon.

description: The white gold of the Terai—cotton is grown for its fiber, which is used in the textile industry. The fluffy white bolls are a common sight in the Terai during the harvest season.
fun_facts: Cotton has been cultivated for over 5,000 years.
The fiber is used to make clothing and other textiles.
The seeds are a source of cottonseed oil.
trivia: In Nepal, cotton is often grown in rotation with other crops in the Terai.

medicinal_uses: Rich in protein and fiber
unique_characters: Versatile; used as both vegetable and pulse
description: A versatile legume that provides both green pods (as a vegetable) and dried seeds (as a pulse). Cowpea is a common crop in the Terai, where it's grown as a vegetable and as a cover crop.
fun_facts: Cowpea is both a vegetable (green pods) and a pulse (dried seeds).
It's drought-tolerant and improves soil fertility.
It's rich in protein and fiber.
trivia: In Nepal, cowpea is often grown as a vegetable in home gardens.

description: A plant whose leaves are used as a vegetable. It's used as an antispasmodic and for arthritis. In Nepal, it's a lesser-known plant.

trivia: Cowslip is also known as marsh marigold and is toxic if not cooked properly.

description: A thistle whose young shoots are used as a vegetable. It's emetic and tonic. Found in temperate regions, but less known in Nepal.
identification: A thistle with spiny leaves and pink-purple flowers.

trivia: Creeping thistle is considered a weed in many places, but its young shoots are edible and nutritious.

trivia: Wood sorrel has a lemony flavor due to oxalic acid and is used in salads.

description: The aromatic seed that's the soul of Nepali cooking—cumin (jira) is an essential spice used in curries, dals, and spice blends. Its warm, earthy flavor is unmistakable in Nepali cuisine.
fun_facts: Cumin is one of the most widely used spices in the world.
It's rich in iron and has many health benefits.
It's a cool-season crop that grows in the Terai.
trivia: In Nepal, cumin is often roasted and ground fresh to maximize its flavor.

description: A shrub whose leaves are used as a flavoring and vegetable in South Asian cuisines. In Nepal, it's called karry patta and is used for stomach disorders.

trivia: Curry leaves are an essential ingredient in South Indian and Nepali cooking, used for flavoring curries and dals.

description: Also called sugar-apple, sarfia has a custardy texture and a sweet, pleasant flavor. It thrives in Nepal's cool temperate regions, where it produces fruits that are highly prized. The fruit is often eaten fresh, but it's also used to make wine and for medicinal purposes. It's a tropical treat that has found a home in the hills.
identification: A small, deciduous tree reaching 3–5 m with thin, oval leaves. The fruit is round to oval, 5–10 cm in diameter, with a green, knobby skin that separates easily. Inside is creamy white flesh with many black seeds.
habitat: Grows in tropical and subtropical climates, often at higher altitudes in Nepal. Found in gardens and orchards in cool temperate regions.
fun_facts: Grows 3–5 m tall. Fruits are 5–10 cm in diameter. Flowering occurs in March-April. Rich in vitamin C and minerals. Native to the tropical Americas.
trivia: In Nepal, sarfia is a seasonal fruit available in the hills. In India, it's often used to make milkshakes and ice cream. The plant has medicinal uses, including treatment of diarrhea and dysentery.

culinary_uses: Green pods cooked as vegetable; dried seeds as dal
medicinal_uses: Rich in protein and fiber
unique_characters: Large seeds; nitrogen-fixing
description: A broad bean with large, flat seeds that are eaten as a vegetable (green) or as a pulse (dried). Faba beans are a traditional crop in Nepal's mid-hills, often grown in home gardens.
fun_facts: Faba beans have been cultivated for over 8,000 years.
They are nitrogen-fixing and improve soil fertility.
The green pods are eaten as a vegetable.
trivia: In Nepal, faba beans are often cooked with the pods or shelled.

description: A plant whose leaves are used as a vegetable and as a hair tonic. In Ayurveda, it's known as bhringraj and is used for hair growth and liver health. In Nepal, it's a common weed.
identification: A creeping herb with opposite, lanceolate leaves and small white flowers.
habitat: Moist areas in tropical and subtropical regions.
fun_facts: Leaves edible. Used as a hair tonic. Effective for liver injury.
trivia: Bhringraj is a well-known Ayurvedic herb for promoting hair growth and preventing premature greying.

culinary_uses: Seeds as spice; bulb as vegetable
medicinal_uses: Good for digestion; carminative properties
description: The sweet, aromatic spice—fennel seeds (saunf) are used as a spice and as a digestive aid. The bulb is also eaten as a vegetable in some areas. Fennel has a mild, licorice-like flavor.
fun_facts: Fennel is native to the Mediterranean and has been used for thousands of years.
The seeds are used as a spice and as a digestive aid.
The bulb is also edible and is used as a vegetable.
trivia: In Nepal, fennel seeds are often eaten after meals as a digestive aid.

culinary_uses: Fresh leaves as vegetable; dried seeds as spice
medicinal_uses: Good for digestion; helps control blood sugar
unique_characters: Nitrogen-fixing; bitter taste (removed by soaking)
description: A versatile plant used as a spice and vegetable—fenugreek (methi) is used in Nepali cooking. The fresh leaves are eaten as a vegetable, and the dried seeds are used as a spice in curries and dals.
fun_facts: Fenugreek has been used in cooking and medicine for thousands of years.
The seeds are rich in iron and other minerals.
It's a nitrogen-fixing plant that improves soil fertility.
trivia: In Nepal, fenugreek seeds are often soaked in water to reduce their bitterness before cooking.

culinary_uses: Fresh green peas as vegetable; dried peas as dal
medicinal_uses: Rich in protein and fiber
unique_characters: Cool-weather crop; nitrogen-fixing
description: A popular cool-weather vegetable and pulse. Field peas are grown in Nepal's hills and Terai, providing fresh green peas in winter and dried peas for dal.
fun_facts: Peas are one of the oldest cultivated crops, dating back to 7,000 BC.
They are nitrogen-fixing and improve soil fertility.
Fresh green peas are a popular winter vegetable.
trivia: In Nepal, fresh green peas are often used in curries and snacks.

description: A soft, sweet fruit with a unique texture—figs are one of the oldest cultivated fruits. They have been grown for over 5,000 years and are a common sight in Nepal's mid-hill gardens. From the Mediterranean to the Middle East, figs have been a symbol of abundance and fertility throughout history.
identification: A deciduous tree reaching 5–10 m with large, lobed leaves. The fruit is a syconium, 3–6 cm long, pear-shaped, with green to purple skin and sweet, edible flesh containing numerous tiny seeds.
habitat: Grows in temperate climates. Found in gardens and orchards in the mid-hills. Prefers well-drained, loamy soil and full sun.
fun_facts: Grows 5–10 m tall. Fruits are 3–6 cm long. Cultivated for over 5,000 years. Rich in fiber and minerals. Figs were among the first cultivated fruits in the ancient Mediterranean.
trivia: Figs are actually inverted flowers—the 'fruit' is a hollow receptacle containing hundreds of tiny flowers and seeds. In Nepal, they are often eaten fresh or dried for winter. In Greece, figs were considered sacred to the goddess Demeter.

culinary_uses: Ground into flour for dhindo, porridge; fermented for tongba
medicinal_uses: Rich in calcium; used for bone health
unique_characters: Extremely high calcium content (3x that of milk); drought-tolerant
cultural_significance: Essential for tongba (millet beer) in Limbu and Rai communities
description: The little grain that could—finger millet is the backbone of Nepal's high-altitude agriculture. It grows where other cereals fail, on thin soils and steep slopes. Kodo is the grain of the hills, the one that fills the stomach when the rice runs low.
fun_facts: Finger millet is one of the oldest cultivated cereals in Africa and Asia.
It has been grown in Nepal for thousands of years.
The grain is rich in calcium, with more than three times the calcium content of milk.
trivia: In the eastern hills of Nepal, finger millet is fermented to make tongba, a warm, nourishing drink that is a staple of social gatherings.

description: A palm tree whose pith and young shoots are edible. It's used for making fibre and also for buttons and beads. In Nepal, it's found in the lower hills, and its sap can be used to make palm wine.
identification: A tall palm with feathery, fishtail-shaped leaves.
fun_facts: Pith and shoots edible. Used for fibre and beads.
trivia: The fishtail palm gets its name from the shape of its leaves. In some regions, its sap is fermented to make toddy.

description: A popular ornamental with edible leaves. In Nepal, its leaves are used as a vegetable. However, roots, seeds, and fruits can be poisonous.
identification: A bushy plant with trumpet-shaped flowers of various colors, and dark green leaves.
habitat: Cultivated in tropical and subtropical regions.
fun_facts: Leaves edible with caution. Ornamental plant. Used for diabetes.
trivia: The Four O'Clock plant is called so because its flowers open in the late afternoon. All parts are mildly toxic.

culinary_uses: Cooked as porridge
medicinal_uses: Nutritious grain; good for digestion
unique_characters: One of the oldest cultivated cereals in Asia; drought-tolerant
conservation_status: Declining; being replaced by other cereals
description: A small grain with a big history—foxtail millet was one of the first cereals domesticated in Asia. In Nepal, it's a traditional crop of the mid-hills, often grown on marginal lands where other cereals struggle.
fun_facts: Foxtail millet is one of the oldest cultivated cereals in Asia, with evidence dating back to 8,000 BC in China.
It is highly nutritious, rich in protein and minerals.
In Nepal, it's often grown as a rain-fed crop in the hills.
trivia: In China, foxtail millet was a staple food before rice became dominant.

A fast-growing green, garden cress is used as a vegetable and spice. In Nepal, it's called chamsur and is often grown in home gardens. The shoots are eaten fresh or cooked.
identification: A small annual herb with pinnate leaves and white or pink flowers.
habitat: Cultivated in temperate and subtropical regions.
fun_facts: Shoots edible. Used as a vegetable and spice. Fast-growing.
trivia: Garden cress is often grown as a microgreen. It has a peppery taste and is rich in vitamins.

culinary_uses: Used fresh, dried, or powdered as a spice
medicinal_uses: Antimicrobial, helps with heart health and digestion
cultural_significance: Used in traditional medicine and religious ceremonies
description: The pungent powerhouse—garlic is an essential spice in Nepali cooking. Its strong flavor and aroma add depth to curries, pickles, and meat dishes. Garlic is also a traditional remedy for many ailments.
fun_facts: Garlic has been used medicinally for over 5,000 years.
It contains allicin, a compound with antimicrobial properties.
Nepal produces several varieties of garlic adapted to different altitudes.
trivia: In Nepal, garlic is often eaten raw with meals as a digestive aid.

culinary_uses: Fresh in curries and tea; dried as spice; pickled
medicinal_uses: Good for digestion, nausea, and colds
unique_characters: Pungent, warming flavor; high in gingerol
cultural_significance: Essential in Nepali cooking and traditional medicine
description: The spicy root that warms every Nepali kitchen—ginger (aduwa) is used in curries, teas, and pickles. It's a staple in traditional medicine and is known for its digestive and warming properties.
fun_facts: Ginger has been used in Asia for over 3,000 years.
It's rich in gingerol, the compound that gives it its spicy flavor.
It's a tropical plant that grows well in Nepal's Terai.
trivia: In Nepal, ginger tea (aduwa ko chai) is a popular home remedy for colds and coughs.

description: A plant whose leaves are used to treat cuts and wounds. In Nepal, it's a common weed with medicinal properties. It's also used for stomachache.
identification: A herb with opposite, hairy leaves and blue flowers.
habitat: Tropical and subtropical regions, in disturbed areas.
fun_facts: Leaves used for wounds. Decoction for stomachache.
trivia: Ageratum is known for its ability to produce a blue dye from its flowers.

description: A wild gooseberry found in Nepal, valued for its high vitamin C content. It's used in traditional medicine, pickles, and candies. Unlike the Indian gooseberry (amla), this is a different species.
identification: A small tree reaching 5–10 m with oval, glossy leaves. The fruit is small, round, 1–2 cm in diameter, with a greenish-yellow skin and sour flesh.
habitat: Grows in tropical and subtropical forests from Terai to mid-hill.
fun_facts: Grows 5–10 m tall. Fruits are 1–2 cm in diameter. Rich in vitamin C. Used in medicine.
trivia: In Nepal, this gooseberry is less known than amla, but it's similarly used for its health benefits. The fruits are also made into pickles and chutneys.

culinary_uses: Ground into flour for flatbreads; popped like popcorn
medicinal_uses: Gluten-free; high in protein and lysine
unique_characters: High-quality protein with lysine; gluten-free
cultural_significance: Traditional grain of the hills
description: The ancient grain of the Aztecs that found a home in Nepal's hills—amaranth is a nutritional powerhouse. Its tiny seeds are ground into flour or popped like popcorn, and its leaves are used as a vegetable.
fun_facts: Amaranth was a staple food of the Aztecs and other Mesoamerican cultures.
It has more protein than most cereals and is rich in lysine.
The seeds can be popped like popcorn.
trivia: In Nepal, amaranth is often grown on marginal lands and is valued for its nutritional content.

description: Hidden among the rocks of the Himalayan foothills, the grape fern appears in the most unexpected places—on cliffs where moss clings, in cracks where dust has settled. Its young leaves can be eaten raw or cooked, and healers use it to treat fever and wounds. It's a small plant with a big role in mountain life.
identification: A small, fleshy fern with a single frond that is divided into two parts: a sterile leaf blade and a fertile spore-bearing stalk. The young leaves are the edible portion.
habitat: Grows in exposed, humid places, often on rocky walls and cliffs where humus has accumulated. Found at elevations from 1,500–3,000 m.
fun_facts: Found at elevations from 1,500–3,000 m. Grows on rocky walls and cliffs. Eaten raw or cooked. Used in traditional medicine for multiple ailments.
trivia: Grape ferns are unusual among ferns because they have a fleshy texture and are sometimes mistaken for small flowering plants. The genus name Botrychium comes from the Greek word for 'grape cluster,' referring to the spore-bearing structure.

uses: Fresh, wine, raisins, jam, juice, jelly, vinegar
description: One of the oldest cultivated fruits, grapes have been grown for over 8,000 years. In Nepal's mid-hills, vineyards are beginning to flourish, producing unique varieties that are increasingly used for wine-making. The sweet berries are a pleasure fresh, dried, or fermented. From the vineyards of Bordeaux to the table grapes of California, grapes are a global treasure.
identification: A woody, climbing vine with large, lobed leaves and coiled tendrils. The fruit grows in hanging clusters (bunches) of 10–50 berries. Each berry is round to oval, 1–2 cm in diameter, with thin skin and juicy flesh containing 2–4 seeds.
habitat: Thrives in temperate and subtropical climates. Found in orchards and vineyards in the mid-hills. Prefers well-drained, loamy soil and full sun.
fun_facts: Grows as a climbing vine. Cultivated for over 8,000 years. One of the most widely grown fruits globally. Rich in antioxidants like resveratrol. There are over 10,000 grape varieties worldwide.
trivia: Nepal's mid-hills produce unique grape varieties for wine-making. The Kakani area near Kathmandu is known for its small-scale vineyards. In Georgia, grape cultivation and wine-making have been practiced for 8,000 years and are part of UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage.

culinary_uses: Cooked as dal
medicinal_uses: Rich in protein (with caution - contains neurotoxin)
unique_characters: Extremely drought-tolerant; contains neurotoxin (must be processed)
description: A hardy pulse that grows in drought-prone areas where other crops fail. Grasspea is a minor crop in Nepal, valued for its ability to grow in poor soils and dry conditions. However, it contains a neurotoxin that must be removed through proper processing.
fun_facts: Grasspea is extremely drought-tolerant and can grow in poor soils.
It contains a neurotoxin (ODAP) that must be removed by soaking and cooking.
It's a source of protein in food-scarce areas.
trivia: Grasspea is often grown as a famine crop because it can survive drought.

culinary_uses: Boiled, curried, fried
medicinal_uses: Good source of carbohydrates and fiber
unique_characters: Large tubers; climbing vine
description: A climbing vine with large, edible tubers. Greater yam is a traditional crop in Nepal, where the tubers are used as a vegetable. It's a good source of carbohydrates and fiber.
fun_facts: Greater yam is one of the most important yam species globally.
The tubers can grow very large, sometimes over 30 kg.
It's a climbing vine that requires support.
trivia: In Nepal, greater yam is often grown on trellises. In the Philippines, it's a staple food.

culinary_uses: Cooked as dal; sprouted as salad; ground into flour
medicinal_uses: Easy to digest; good for health
unique_characters: Quick-maturing; nitrogen-fixing
description: A small, green pulse that's a favorite in Nepali kitchens. Green gram is quick-cooking and easy to digest, making it a popular dal. The sprouted seeds are used in salads and stir-fries.
fun_facts: Green gram is one of the most important pulse crops in Nepal.
It's quick-maturing, maturing in 75-90 days.
The sprouts are highly nutritious and rich in vitamins.
trivia: In Chinese cuisine, mung beans are used to make noodles and desserts.

culinary_uses: Oil for cooking; roasted seeds as snack; peanut butter
medicinal_uses: Rich in healthy fats and protein
unique_characters: Fruits mature underground; nitrogen-fixing
description: A legume that produces its fruits underground—groundnuts are a valuable oilseed and snack. In Nepal, groundnuts are grown in the Terai and are eaten roasted or used to make oil.
fun_facts: Groundnuts, also known as peanuts, are not true nuts—they're legumes.
The fruits mature underground, which is unique among legumes.
They are a good source of protein and healthy fats.
trivia: In Nepal, groundnuts are often roasted in their shells and sold as a snack.

culinary_uses: Fresh, in juice, in jam
medicinal_uses: Rich in vitamin C and antioxidants
description: The tropical fruit that's a favorite in Nepal—guava (amba) is a sweet, fragrant fruit. It's eaten fresh, used in juice, and made into jam and jelly.
fun_facts: Guava is native to the Americas.
It's rich in vitamin C.
The fruit is used fresh, in juice, and in preserves.
trivia: In Nepal, guava is often eaten fresh with salt and chili powder.

When spring comes to the Himalayan foothills, young shoots of this shrub appear—tender and green, ready to be cooked as a vegetable. Its dark berries are sweet and edible, and its leaves and fruit have been used for generations to bring down fevers. Like its relatives in Europe, this elderberry plant is both food and medicine.
identification: A deciduous shrub reaching 1–3 m with compound leaves and clusters of small white flowers. The fruits are small, dark berries. The young shoots are the edible portion.
habitat: Grows in temperate regions, often in forests, forest edges, and along streams. Found in the Himalayas.
fun_facts: Grows 1–3 m tall. Fruits are edible and sweet. Used in traditional medicine. Found in the Himalayas.
trivia: Elderberries are commonly used to make wine and syrup in many parts of the world, including Europe and North America. In Nepal, the young shoots are valued as a spring vegetable. In European folklore, elder trees are said to protect against evil spirits.

description: Named after the Danish botanist Nathaniel Wallich, this wild garlic is one of the most flavorful of Nepal's alliums. Its leaves and bulbs are used as a vegetable and spice, and it's been shown to have antimicrobial properties. In the mountain communities, it's a precious resource—both food and medicine.
identification: A perennial herb with garlic-like leaves and bulbs. The leaves and bulbs are the edible portions.
habitat: Grows in temperate and alpine regions of the Himalayas. Found in meadows, forests, and rocky slopes.
fun_facts: Found in the Himalayas. Has antimicrobial properties. Used as a vegetable. Harvested in August-October.
trivia: This wild garlic is named after the Danish botanist Nathaniel Wallich, who was the first to describe many of the plants of the Himalayas. It is considered one of the most flavorful wild alliums in Nepal. In China, it's used in traditional medicine.

culinary_uses: Cooked as dal; sprouted
medicinal_uses: Good for kidney health
unique_characters: Highly drought-tolerant; grows in poor soils
cultural_significance: Traditional food; used in festivals
description: A hardy pulse that grows in poor soils and dry conditions. Horse gram is a traditional food of Nepal's hills, often cooked as dal and eaten with rice. It's also used as animal feed.
fun_facts: Horse gram is highly drought-tolerant and can grow in poor soils.
It's a good source of protein and iron.
It's often used in traditional medicine for kidney health.
trivia: In Nepal, horse gram is often eaten during the winter months.
