uses: Fruit pulp edible, cooked as vegetable
description: Another barberry species, chutro, found in tropical and subtropical areas of Nepal. Its bright red berries are both edible and used in cooking—the pulp is cooked as a vegetable or made into chutney. It shares the medicinal properties of its relatives, used for skin ailments and digestive issues.
identification: An evergreen shrub with spiny branches and clusters of red berries. The fruit is similar to B. asiatica, but the plant is found at lower elevations.
habitat: Grows in tropical and subtropical regions, often in open forests and along roadsides.
fun_facts: Found in tropical and subtropical regions. Fruit pulp is edible. Used as a vegetable. Related to B. asiatica.
trivia: In some parts of Nepal, the berries are sun-dried and used as a spice or souring agent. The plant is also used as a hedge due to its thorns.

description: Also known as chiuri, this tree yields a butter-like fat from its seeds, used in cooking and medicine. The fruit is also edible. It's a valuable tree for hill communities.
identification: A medium-sized tree reaching 8–15 m with thick, leathery leaves. The fruit is a large berry containing a seed rich in fat.
habitat: Grows in subtropical and temperate forests at 600–1,500 m.
fun_facts: Grows 8–15 m tall. Seeds yield butter. Used as a vegetable.
trivia: In Nepal, the butter is used for cooking, as a hair oil, and in lamps. The fruit is also eaten fresh. The tree is often conserved in community forests.

description: Also called the Himalayan mango, amaro is a wild relative of the mango with a sour, tangy flavor. It grows in the mid-hills, often found in forests and along stream banks. The fruit is eaten fresh when ripe, its sweet-sour pulp a refreshing snack for those who know where to find it.
identification: A medium-sized deciduous tree reaching 6–20 m with a smooth, aromatic bark. The fruit is small, oval, 3–5 cm long, with yellow skin and sour, fibrous flesh containing a single seed.
habitat: Grows in tropical and subtropical forests, often along streams and in moist areas. Found in the mid-hills of Nepal.
fun_facts: Grows 6–20 m tall. Fruits are 3–5 cm long. Related to the mango. The bark is aromatic. Flowering occurs in March-April.
trivia: In Nepal, amaro is a wild fruit gathered from forests. Its sourness makes it a favorite for pickles and chutneys. In South India, a similar species is used in traditional cooking.

description: A tree with long, pod-like fruits used in traditional medicine for constipation. In Nepal, it's called rajbrikshya and is a common ornamental.
identification: A medium-sized tree with long, pendulous clusters of yellow flowers and long, cylindrical pods.
fun_facts: Fruits used for constipation. Ornamental tree.
trivia: Indian laburnum is known for its stunning golden flowers and is the national tree of Thailand.

description: A fern with a unique appearance—its fronds are interrupted by fertile leaflets in the middle, as if someone cut them and pasted them back differently. In Nepal, it's not commonly eaten, but in North America, it was a food of the Native peoples. The center of the clump yields a small edible pith they called 'fern butter'—a name that speaks of its creamy texture and value.
identification: A large fern with broad, divided fronds growing up to 1 m tall. The fronds have a distinctive interrupted appearance due to the fertile leaflets in the middle. The young fronds are the edible portion.
habitat: Grows in moist, wooded areas, often along streams and in swampy forests. Found in temperate regions of North America and Asia.
fun_facts: Fronds can grow up to 1 m tall. Found in temperate regions of North America and Asia. The pith is called 'fern butter'. Named for its interrupted fronds.
trivia: This fern gets its common name from the way its fertile leaflets interrupt the green leaf blade. It was used by Native Americans as a food source, who valued the edible pith from the center of the clump.

description: A climbing plant with edible fruits, ivy gourd is used as a vegetable. In Nepal, it's called golkankri and is valued for its medicinal properties, including treatment of leprosy and asthma.
identification: A vine with ivy-like leaves and small, red-orange, oblong fruits.
fun_facts: Fruits edible. Used for leprosy and asthma.
trivia: Ivy gourd is a common vegetable in South Asian and Southeast Asian cuisines. It's also used in traditional medicine for diabetes.

uses: Fresh bulbs, cooked, seeds boiled/roasted, curries, jams, nectars, chips, dehydrated leather
description: The largest tree-borne fruit in the world—a single jackfruit can feed an entire village. This tropical marvel has been cultivated for centuries and is now celebrated as a meat substitute in kitchens from Portland to Paris. In rural Terai gardens, these fruits hang like green monsters, promising a feast within their spiky armor.
identification: A large evergreen tree reaching 15–25 m with thick, dark green, oblong leaves. The fruit is massive and oblong, 4–27 kg or more, covered in a green, spiky rind. Inside are sweet, yellow bulbs surrounding large seeds.
habitat: Grows in tropical lowlands and foothills. Found in home gardens, orchards, and roadsides. Prefers well-drained, fertile soil and full sun.
fun_facts: Grows up to 25 m tall. Fruits weigh 4–27 kg. Trees begin bearing in 3–5 years. One tree produces 100–200 fruits per year. The largest recorded jackfruit weighed over 40 kg and was grown in Sri Lanka.
trivia: A single jackfruit can contain up to 500 edible bulbs. In Nepal, oil your hands and knife before cutting—the sticky sap is almost impossible to wash off with water alone. In Southeast Asia, jackfruit is used in desserts, curries, and even as a meat substitute in vegan dishes.

culinary_uses: Fresh ripe fruit, unripe fruit as vegetable, seeds cooked
medicinal_uses: Rich in carbohydrates and antioxidants
cultural_significance: Important during festivals
description: The giant of the fruit world—jackfruit (rukh kathar) is a massive fruit that grows on trees in Nepal's Terai. The sweet, yellow flesh is eaten fresh, and the unripe fruit is used as a vegetable.
fun_facts: Jackfruit is the largest tree-borne fruit in the world.
Both the ripe fruit and unripe fruit are edible.
The seeds are also edible when cooked.
trivia: In Nepal, jackfruit is often cooked as a vegetable when unripe, and eaten fresh when ripe.

uses: Fresh, sherbets, jams, traditional diabetes remedies
description: A fruit that stains your tongue purple—Jamun is a summer treat known for its sweet-tart flavor and deep purple color. It has been used in traditional medicine for diabetes management for centuries. From India to Indonesia, jamun is a beloved monsoon fruit with a rich cultural history.
identification: A large evergreen tree reaching 15–30 m with glossy, oblong leaves and fragrant flowers. The fruit is a berry, 2–3 cm long, oblong, with smooth, deep purple to black skin and greenish-white flesh surrounding a single seed.
habitat: Grows in tropical and subtropical climates. Found in Terai forests, gardens, and along roadsides. Prefers well-drained, loamy soil and full sun.
fun_facts: Grows 15–30 m tall. Fruits are 2–3 cm long. The fruit stains the tongue purple. Traditionally used for diabetes. The tree is native to the Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia.
trivia: Jamun is known as the 'fruit of the gods' in traditional Indian medicine. In Nepal, the fruits are a common sight at market stalls during monsoon. In Bangladesh, jamun is used to make a popular summer drink called 'jambura sharbat.'

description: A fern that has traveled far from its Asian homeland, now growing wild in countries where it was never meant to be. In Nepal, its young leaves are still gathered, but in places like Florida and the Deep South, it has become an unwelcome invader—a reminder of how plants, like people, can leave home and change the world in unexpected ways.
identification: A climbing fern with twining fronds that can grow several meters long. The leaves are divided into small leaflets. The very young leaves are the edible portion.
habitat: Grows in tropical and subtropical forests, often climbing over other vegetation. Found in moist, shaded areas.
fun_facts: Can climb several meters in height. Native to Asia. Spores used in traditional medicine. Harvested in May-June.
trivia: This fern is considered an invasive species in parts of the southeastern United States, where it can smother native vegetation. In traditional Chinese medicine, its spores are used for urinary discomfort.

description: A plant whose leaves are used as an antipyretic and for detoxification. In Nepal, it's a lesser-known medicinal herb.
identification: A herb with pinnatifid leaves and yellow flowers.
fun_facts: Leaves used as antipyretic. Found in Nepal.
trivia: Youngia species are sometimes used as a substitute for lettuce in salads.

description: A spice that is uniquely Nepali—jimbu has a strong garlic-onion flavor and is used in soups, dals, and vegetable dishes across the country. It's difficult to find outside Nepal, and those who know it crave its distinctive taste. Dried jimbu is a pantry staple, a taste of home for those who have traveled far.
identification: A perennial herb with onion-like leaves and bulbs. The leaves are the primary edible portion.
habitat: Grows in temperate and alpine regions of the Himalayas. Found in meadows and rocky slopes.
fun_facts: Found in the Himalayas. Used as a spice. Has a strong garlic-onion flavor. Dried leaves used as seasoning.
trivia: Jimbu is a prized spice in Nepalese cuisine, especially in the mountainous regions where it is often used to flavor soups, dals, and vegetable dishes. It is difficult to find outside of Nepal and is a valued export. In China, similar wild alliums are used in traditional cuisines.

uses: Fresh, sun-dried, preserves, traditional snacks, pickled, beverages
description: A hardy fruit that thrives in dry, hot conditions where other fruits struggle. Jujube is a common sight in the Terai, where its sweet, apple-like fruits ripen in late winter and spring. From Africa to Southeast Asia, jujube has been a vital food source in arid regions for centuries.
identification: A spiny, evergreen to semi-evergreen shrub or small tree reaching 3–10 m with oval leaves. The fruit is round to oval, 2–5 cm in diameter, with smooth, edible skin that ripens from green to yellow or brown. The flesh is sweet, dry, and floury.
habitat: Thrives in dry, tropical and subtropical climates. Found in Terai gardens, roadsides, and waste areas. Prefers well-drained, sandy soil and full sun.
fun_facts: Grows 3–10 m tall. Fruits are 2–5 cm in diameter. Thrives in dry, hot conditions. Rich in vitamin C and minerals. The jujube has been cultivated in South Asia and Africa for over 4,000 years.
trivia: Jujube is one of the few fruits that can grow with minimal water. In Nepal's Terai, it's often found growing along roadsides in dry, marginal lands. In China, jujube (called 'hong zao') is a traditional remedy for insomnia and anxiety.

description: A tree with edible fruits, used as a snack and in traditional medicine. In Nepal, it's called bayer and is used as a tonic and laxative.
identification: A small tree with spiny branches and small, oval, reddish-brown fruits.
fun_facts: Fruits edible. Used as a laxative. Purifies blood.
trivia: Jujube fruits are often dried and used as a sweet snack. They are also used in Chinese medicine.

It's biodegradable and eco-friendly.
The leaves are also edible and are used as a vegetable.
trivia: In Nepal, jute is sometimes used to make traditional sacks for storing grains.

Tiny tart berries that pack a punch—karonda is the sharp tang that wakes up your taste buds. They grow on a shrub that often doubles as a hedge, their red to black fruits hiding among the thorns. In Nepal's Terai, they are mostly pickled, their sourness balanced with salt and spices. In India, they are used to make a sweet sauce. A humble berry with a fierce flavor.
identification: A spiny shrub reaching 1–2 m with opposite, oval leaves. The fruit is a small, oval berry, 1–2 cm long, ripening from red to deep purple-black. The flesh is tart and astringent.
habitat: Grows in tropical and subtropical climates. Found in gardens, hedgerows, and roadsides. Prefers well-drained soil and full sun.
fun_facts: Grows 1–2 m tall. Fruits are 1–2 cm long. Often used in pickles. Rich in vitamin C. The shrub is drought-tolerant and used as a living fence.
trivia: In Nepal, karonda is a common hedge plant. The ripe berries are often made into a spicy pickle that's eaten with meals. In Ayurveda, the fruit is used for its digestive properties.

description: The cultivated kiwifruit, now grown in Nepal's mid-hills. It's a recent introduction but has become popular due to its tangy-sweet flavor and high vitamin C content. The fuzzy brown fruit hides bright green flesh with tiny black seeds.
identification: A climbing vine with hairy leaves and large, oval fruits with brown, fuzzy skin. The flesh is green with a white core and small black seeds.
habitat: Grows in temperate climates with well-drained soil. Found in orchards in the mid-hills.
fun_facts: A climbing vine. Fruits are 5–8 cm long. Rich in vitamin C. Cultivated in Nepal.
trivia: Kiwifruit was originally called Chinese gooseberry. In Nepal, it's a high-value crop, exported to India and beyond. The fruit is also used in jams and desserts.

description: A versatile bean grown for its edible pods and seeds. Lablab bean is a traditional crop in Nepal, often grown as a vegetable in home gardens and as a pulse in the fields.
fun_facts: Lablab bean is also known as hyacinth bean.
It's a perennial plant that can produce for several years.
Both the pods and seeds are edible and nutritious.
trivia: In Nepal, lablab bean is often grown on trellises in home gardens.

description: A fern with a surprising superpower—it drinks up arsenic like a thirsty traveler. This ability has made it a hero in environmental cleanups, sucking toxins from contaminated soil. In some places, its rhizome is eaten as a tonic, but caution is wise; the fern absorbs heavy metals and stores them in its tissues. It's a reminder that wild food is always a careful balance of benefit and risk.
identification: A medium-sized fern with dark green, divided fronds. The young shoots and rhizomes are the edible portion. The plant has a short, creeping rhizome.
habitat: Grows in tropical and subtropical regions, often on walls, rocks, and disturbed areas. Found in Asia, Africa, and the Americas.
fun_facts: Known for hyperaccumulating arsenic. Found on walls and rocks. Used for environmental remediation. Found in Asia, Africa, and the Americas.
trivia: This fern is so efficient at absorbing arsenic that it's been used to clean up contaminated sites. It can accumulate up to 7,500 parts per million of arsenic in its fronds. In India, it's sometimes used as a medicinal plant.

description: A weed that has fed the world—lamb's quarters grows on every continent, a wild green that is more nutritious than spinach. In Nepal, it's called bethe, a common vegetable during the cooler months. Its tiny seeds can be ground into flour, and its leaves are a staple of rural diets. It's the plant that refuses to be forgotten.
identification: An annual herb reaching 0.3–1.5 m with diamond-shaped, mealy leaves. The young shoots and leaves are the edible portion.
habitat: Grows in temperate regions worldwide. Found in disturbed areas, fields, gardens, and along roadsides.
fun_facts: Grows 0.3–1.5 m tall. Found worldwide in temperate regions. Seeds can be ground into flour. Used in traditional medicine.
trivia: Lamb's quarters are highly nutritious, containing more iron and calcium than spinach. The plant was a staple food for many Native American tribes and is still used as a wild green in many cultures. In Nepal, it's a common vegetable during the winter months.

Tiny and delicate, this fern is easy to overlook—a mere finger's length in height. Its name comes from its spore stalk, which looks like a tongue. In some places, it's gathered as food, but in Nepal, it's a curiosity rather than a staple, a reminder that even the smallest plants have their place in the wild kitchen.

fun_facts: Grows only 5–15 cm tall. Found in tropical and subtropical regions. Used in traditional medicine in Africa. Sometimes grown as an ornamental.
trivia: Adder's tongue ferns are among the smallest ferns in the world. The name comes from the spore-bearing stalk, which resembles a snake's tongue. In traditional African medicine, a decoction of its rhizomes is used to treat stomach disorders.

trivia: Houttuynia is a popular vegetable in some Asian cuisines and is also used in traditional medicine for its health benefits.

description: A sweet, early-spring fruit that arrives when the weather is just beginning to warm. Loquat is a popular backyard tree in Nepal's mid-hills, valued for its delicious, tangy-sweet fruits. From China to the Mediterranean, loquats are a cherished sign of spring's arrival.
identification: A small evergreen tree reaching 5–10 m with large, glossy, serrated leaves. The fruit is oval, 3–5 cm long, with smooth, yellow to orange skin and sweet, tangy, orange flesh containing 1–2 large seeds.
habitat: Grows in temperate and subtropical climates. Found in gardens and orchards in the mid-hills and Kathmandu Valley. Prefers well-drained, loamy soil and full sun.
fun_facts: Grows 5–10 m tall. Fruits are 3–5 cm long. One of the earliest spring fruits. Rich in vitamins A and C. Loquats are native to China and have been cultivated for over 1,000 years.
trivia: Loquat leaves are used in traditional medicine to treat respiratory conditions. In Nepal, the fruit is often eaten fresh as the first taste of spring. In Spain, loquats are used to make a sweet, thick syrup called 'jarabe de níspero.'

Macadamia nuts are a recent addition to Nepal's agriculture, grown in the mid-hills. The nuts are rich and buttery, often eaten roasted or used in baking. The tree is subtropical and requires a warm, frost-free climate.
identification: A medium-sized evergreen tree reaching 10–15 m with glossy, oblong leaves. The fruit is a hard-shelled nut, round, 1–2 cm in diameter, with a creamy kernel.
habitat: Grows in subtropical climates, in well-drained soil. Found in orchards in the mid-hills.
fun_facts: Grows 10–15 m tall. Nuts are 1–2 cm in diameter. Rich and buttery flavor. A recent introduction to Nepal.
trivia: Macadamia nuts are native to Australia. In Nepal, they are a high-value export crop. The nuts are also used in chocolates and ice creams.

description: A semi-deciduous tree with a sour reputation—its fruits are used as a condiment in pickles and spice blends. The plant is related to sumac, and its tart flavor adds depth to local dishes. In Nepal, it's a lesser-known ingredient, but those who know it appreciate its unique tang.
identification: A semi-deciduous tree reaching up to 6 m with compound leaves and greenish-yellow flowers. The fruit is small, round, and covered in short hairs, with a sour taste.
habitat: Grows in tropical and subtropical forests, often in open areas and along roadsides. Found in the mid-hills.
fun_facts: Grows up to 6 m tall. Used as a spice. Related to sumac. Flowering occurs in March-July.
trivia: The fruit of this plant is sometimes used as a substitute for sumac in cooking. In Nepal, it's called bakiamilo and is a traditional seasoning. The plant is also used in traditional medicine.

A climbing fern that weaves through the forest undergrowth, its delicate tendrils reaching ever upward. Its young shoots are a favorite green, and its leaves have been used for generations as medicine—crushed and applied to snake bites, or brewed for jaundice. It's a plant that both feeds and heals.
identification: A climbing fern with twining fronds that can grow several meters long. The leaves are divided into small leaflets. The young shoots are the edible portion.
habitat: Grows in tropical and subtropical forests, often climbing over other vegetation. Found in moist, shaded areas.
fun_facts: Can climb several meters in height. Harvested throughout the year. Used in traditional medicine for jaundice and wounds. Leaves used for insect and snake bites.
trivia: This fern's climbing habit is unusual among ferns, which typically grow as upright or creeping plants. Its long, twining fronds can reach up to 10 meters in length. In Southeast Asia, similar climbing ferns are used for medicinal purposes.

flower_color: Male flowers in tassel; female in ear (cob)
culinary_uses: Roasted green ears, ground into flour for dhindo, porridge
medicinal_uses: Corn silk used as diuretic
economic_importance: Third most important cereal; covers ~23% of cropped area
description: The hill farmer's best friend—maize grows where rice and wheat struggle, climbing up the steep slopes of Nepal's mid-hills. It's the third most important cereal in Nepal, covering about 23% of the cropped area.
fun_facts: Nepal produces about 2.5 million metric tons of maize annually.
It is the main staple in the mid-hills, where it often replaces rice as the primary food.
The crop is also vital for animal feed, with the stalks used as fodder.
trivia: Maize was domesticated in Mexico over 9,000 years ago and has since spread to every continent. In Nepal, maize is often intercropped with beans and squash, a traditional farming practice that mimics the 'Three Sisters' method of Native American agriculture.

description: A shrub that has been a trusted healer for centuries—in Ayurveda, it's known as 'vasaka' and used to clear the lungs and soothe bronchitis. Its leaves, when boiled, are eaten with salt in some parts of India, a practice that has crossed borders into Nepal. It's also planted in fields as green manure, enriching the soil as it heals the body.
identification: An evergreen shrub reaching 2–4 m with opposite, lance-shaped leaves and white or purple flowers. The leaves are the primary edible part.
habitat: Grows in tropical and subtropical regions, often in gardens and along roadsides. Found in Asia.
fun_facts: Grows 2–4 m tall. Used in traditional medicine. Grown as a green manure. Found in Asia.
trivia: In Ayurvedic medicine, this plant is known as 'vasaka' and has been used for centuries to treat respiratory conditions. The leaves contain alkaloids that help relax the airways. In Nepal, it's commonly found growing wild and in gardens.

description: A climbing plant with succulent leaves used as a spinach substitute. In Nepal, it's called poi sag and is a popular green. It has demulcent and diuretic properties.
identification: A climbing vine with heart-shaped, fleshy leaves.
fun_facts: Leaves used as spinach. Has demulcent properties.
trivia: Malabar spinach is not a true spinach but has a similar taste and texture when cooked. It's a staple in many Asian cuisines.

The most widely grown citrus in Nepal, mandarins are a winter favorite. Their loose, easy-peel skin and sweet, juicy segments make them irresistible. They are the cornerstone of Nepal's fruit industry and a beloved snack during cold months, just as they are in China, Japan, and across the Mediterranean.
identification: A small evergreen tree reaching 4–8 m with glossy, dark green leaves and thornless branches. Fruits are small, 5–8 cm in diameter, with loose, bright orange skin that peels easily. The flesh is sweet, juicy, and divided into 8–12 segments.
habitat: Grows in subtropical climates. Found in orchards and home gardens in the mid-hills. Prefers well-drained, loamy soil and full sun.
fun_facts: Grows 4–8 m tall. Fruits are 5–8 cm in diameter. Nepal produces over 100,000 metric tons annually. An excellent source of vitamin C. China is the world's largest mandarin producer.
trivia: Mandarins are the 'king of citrus fruits' in Nepal. Dhankuta and Sindhuli districts are famous for their high-quality mandarins. In Japan, the mandarin is called 'mikan' and is a beloved winter fruit.

culinary_uses: Fresh, in juice, in desserts
medicinal_uses: Rich in vitamin C; good for immune health
economic_importance: Important fruit crop
description: The small, sweet citrus fruit of the hills—mandarin (junara) is a popular winter fruit in Nepal. Its sweet, fragrant segments are a favorite snack and a symbol of Nepali hospitality.
fun_facts: Mandarin is one of the oldest cultivated citrus fruits.
Nepal's mandarins are known for their sweet flavor.
The fruit is rich in vitamin C.
trivia: In Nepal, mandarins are often given as gifts during festivals.

culinary_uses: Fresh, in juice, pickles, desserts
medicinal_uses: Rich in vitamin C and antioxidants
cultural_significance: National fruit; used in festivals and religious ceremonies
economic_importance: Major fruit crop
description: The king of fruits—mango (aap) is the undisputed monarch of Nepal's summer. The sweet, juicy fruit is a national treasure, and the sight of mango orchards in the Terai is a symbol of abundance.
fun_facts: Mango is the national fruit of India and Pakistan.
Nepal produces over 2 million metric tons of mangoes annually.
There are many varieties of mango, from sweet to fiber-rich.
trivia: In Nepal, mangoes are often eaten with rice and dal during the summer months. Mango pickle (aap ko achar) is a popular condiment.

description: A tree with a powerful reputation—its fruits have been used in traditional medicine for millennia, but they are toxic if not prepared with care. The nut is burned to release oil, which is then used as a remedy for everything from warts to tumors. In Nepal, it's known as bhalayo, a name that carries both respect and caution.
identification: A medium-sized deciduous tree with compound leaves and small, fleshy fruits. The fruits are the primary medicinal portion.
habitat: Grows in tropical and subtropical forests. Found in Asia.
fun_facts: Used in traditional medicine. Toxic if not prepared properly. Harvested in November-February. Found in Asia.
trivia: The fruit of this tree has been used for centuries in traditional medicine to make a powerful remedy called 'bhallatak.' The nut is burned to release the oil, which is then used in various preparations. In Nepal, it's used with extreme caution.

trivia: This plant is also known as 'epazote' in Mexico, where it's commonly used to flavor bean dishes. It's believed to reduce the gas-causing effects of beans. In Nepal, it's used as a medicinal herb and spice.

medicinal_uses: Good for digestion; rich in antioxidants

description: The refreshing herb that's essential in Nepali kitchens—mint (pudina) is used in chutneys, teas, and as a spice. Its fresh, cool flavor is a favorite in traditional medicine and cooking.
fun_facts: Mint has been used for thousands of years in cooking and medicine.
It's rich in antioxidants.
The plant spreads rapidly through underground rhizomes.
trivia: In Nepal, mint is often used in chutney and as a digestive aid.

description: A climbing plant with fragrant night-blooming flowers. Its leaves are used as a vegetable. In Nepal, it's known for its medicinal uses, including snakebite remedy.
identification: A vine with heart-shaped leaves and large, white, fragrant flowers that open at night.
fun_facts: Leaves edible. Used for snakebite. Has fragrant night flowers.
trivia: Moonflower is related to the morning glory and is often grown as an ornamental for its beautiful, scented blossoms.

uses: Fresh, dried, jams, juice, stews, tarts, leaves as vegetable and fodder
description: The tree that feeds silkworms and humans! Mulberry is a common sight across Nepal, growing in gardens, roadsides, and forest edges. Its sweet, messy berries are a summer treat that stain fingers and clothes. From China's ancient silk industry to Europe's traditional orchards, mulberries have played a vital role in human civilization for millennia.
identification: A deciduous tree reaching 5–15 m with rounded, lobed leaves that vary in shape. The fruit is an elongated cluster of tiny berries, 1–2 cm long, ripening from white to pink to dark purple. The sweet, juicy berries stain fingers and clothing.
habitat: Grows in a wide range of climates, from lowland to mid-hills. Found in gardens, roadsides, and field edges. Prefers well-drained soil and full sun.
fun_facts: Grows 5–15 m tall. Fruits are 1–2 cm long. Leaves are the primary food for silkworms. Rich in vitamins and minerals. In China, mulberries have been cultivated for silk production for over 5,000 years.
trivia: Mulberry trees are so versatile that in Nepal, they've been planted at elevations from 200 m to 2,000 m. The dark purple stain from mulberries is notoriously hard to wash off. In Persia, mulberries were traditionally used to make jam and fruit leather.

description: A plant whose fruits are used as a vegetable. In Nepal, it's called latakasturi and is used for nervous troubles.
identification: A herb with palmately lobed leaves and yellow flowers with a dark center.
fun_facts: Fruits edible. Used for nervous issues.
trivia: The seeds have a musky odor and are used in perfumery.

medicinal_uses: Rich in vitamin C and antioxidants

trivia: In Nepal, muskmelon is often eaten fresh as a snack.

description: The most important oilseed crop in Nepal—mustard oil is the cooking oil of choice in most Nepali kitchens. The leaves (rayoko sag) are a popular winter vegetable, and the seeds are used as a spice.
fun_facts: Mustard oil is the primary cooking oil in Nepal.
The leaves (rayoko sag) are a popular winter vegetable.
Mustard is a major cash crop in the Terai.
trivia: In Nepal, mustard oil is used not only for cooking but also for massage and in traditional remedies.

medicinal_uses: Good for digestive health

fun_facts: Naked barley is also known as 'hull-less barley'.
It is easier to process than regular barley because the hull comes off during threshing.
It grows at altitudes up to 4,000 m.
trivia: In Nepal's high Himalayas, naked barley is a staple food for Tibetan communities.

A lily whose bulbs and leaves are used as a vegetable. In Nepal, it's called khiraulo and is used for heart diseases.
identification: A tall lily with large, trumpet-shaped flowers, often greenish-yellow with purple spots.
fun_facts: Bulbs and leaves edible. Used for heart diseases. Found in Nepal.
trivia: Lilium nepalense is a striking species with a unique color, often grown as an ornamental.

description: Timur is the Nepali pepper—a dried berry with a pungent, citrusy, and numbing flavor. It's an essential spice in Nepali cuisine, used in pickles, curries, and even tea. Harvested in mid-September, it's a cash crop for many hill farmers. The berries are dried and sold in markets, their aroma unmistakable.
identification: A spiny, deciduous shrub or small tree reaching 3–5 m with compound leaves and small, reddish-brown berries. The berries are the spice.
habitat: Grows in temperate forests and scrublands at elevations of 1,000–2,500 m. Found in the mid-hills.
fun_facts: Grows 3–5 m tall. Dried berries are used as a spice. Has a numbing, citrusy flavor. Harvested in mid-September. Also used in traditional medicine.
trivia: Timur is often confused with Sichuan pepper—they are in the same genus. In Nepal, timur is a key ingredient in 'momo achar' (dumpling sauce). It's also used to treat indigestion and toothaches.

uses: Bark used for dysentery and toothache, leaf decoction for diarrhoea
description: A pink-flowered shrub native to Nepal, with medicinal uses. Its bark is used for dysentery and toothache, and leaf decoction for diarrhea. It's a lesser-known plant but valued in traditional medicine.
identification: A shrub reaching 1–2 m with pink flowers and hairy leaves.
habitat: Grows in tropical and subtropical areas.
fun_facts: A shrub with pink flowers. Used in traditional medicine. Found in Nepal.
trivia: In Nepal, the plant is used by local healers for gastrointestinal ailments. Its flowers are also ornamental.

description: A yam species found in Nepal, used as a vegetable. The tubers are starchy and nutritious, often cooked in curries. It's a wild plant that is also sometimes cultivated.
identification: A climbing vine with heart-shaped leaves and underground tubers. The tubers are elongated, with a rough skin and white or yellow flesh.
habitat: Grows in temperate forests and on slopes.
fun_facts: A climbing vine. Tubers are used as a vegetable. Found in Nepal. Harvested in November-December.
trivia: In Nepal, this yam is a traditional food, especially during winter. The tubers are also used in traditional medicine for joint pain.

description: Lapsi is the sour heart of the mid-hills—when it ripens, the whole community comes together to make titaura. The fruit has a unique flavor: sour, slightly sweet, and deeply satisfying. Women slice the fruit, dry it in the sun, and turn it into a tangy candy that is a staple in every Nepali household. It's a taste of the hills that you can carry anywhere.
identification: A medium-sized deciduous tree reaching 12–20 m with compound leaves and yellow-green flowers. The fruit is oval, 3–5 cm long, with smooth, yellow skin and sour, fibrous flesh surrounding a single large seed.
habitat: Grows in subtropical and temperate climates. Found in orchards, home gardens, and forest edges in the mid-hills. Prefers well-drained, loamy soil and full sun.
fun_facts: Grows 12–20 m tall. Fruits are 3–5 cm long. Used to make titaura (fruit leather). Rich in vitamins and minerals. The tree is endemic to the Himalayan region.
trivia: In Nepal, lapsi is a cultural icon—no wedding or festival is complete without some titaura. The dried fruit is also exported to India and beyond. The fruit is also used in traditional remedies for digestive disorders.

description: The chiuri tree is a source of edible fat—its seeds yield a butter-like oil that is used in cooking and traditional medicine. The fruit itself is also edible. In the hills, the tree is valued for its many uses. It's a lesser-known but important resource for local communities.
identification: A medium-sized tree reaching 8–15 m with thick, leathery leaves. The fruit is a large, fleshy berry containing a seed that yields butter.
habitat: Grows in subtropical and temperate forests at elevations of 600–1,500 m. Found in the mid-hills and Terai.
fun_facts: Grows 8–15 m tall. Seeds yield a butter-like oil. Used as a vegetable. Important for local communities.
trivia: In Nepal, chiuri butter is used in cooking and also as a hair and skin treatment. The fruit is eaten fresh or cooked. The tree is also planted for its shade and as a fodder source.

description: A cousin of lamb's quarters, this plant is often dismissed as a weed. But its leaves are good eating, and its seeds, like quinoa, are nutritious. In Nepal, it grows in the same disturbed soils as its relative, a wild green that offers food to those who know its worth.
identification: An annual herb reaching 0.3–0.8 m with triangular, mealy leaves. The leaves and seeds are the edible portions.
habitat: Grows in tropical and subtropical regions. Found in disturbed areas, fields, and along roadsides.
fun_facts: Grows 0.3–0.8 m tall. Has antibacterial properties. Seeds edible like quinoa. Found in disturbed areas.
trivia: This plant is named for the similarity of its leaves to those of nettles, but it doesn't have the stinging hairs of nettles. It is a close relative of quinoa. In some countries, it's used as a green manure and animal fodder.

description: An oilseed plant whose seeds are used as a spice and for oil extraction. In Nepal, it's grown as a winter crop. The seeds are also used in cooking.

habitat: Cultivated in tropical and subtropical regions.
fun_facts: Seeds used for oil and spice. Grown in winter.
trivia: Niger seed is commonly used as birdseed and for oil extraction. It's a staple in Ethiopian cuisine as well.

medicinal_uses: Good source of healthy fats

The seeds are a popular birdseed.

description: A sweet-tart stone fruit that comes in many colors and flavors. Plums have been cultivated for thousands of years and are a common sight in Nepal's mid-hill gardens. They are one of the first fruits to ripen after spring. From the orchards of California to the markets of Europe, plums are a beloved summer fruit.
identification: A small deciduous tree reaching 4–8 m with oval, toothed leaves and white flowers in spring. The fruit is round to oval, 3–6 cm in diameter, with smooth, red, purple, or yellow skin and juicy flesh surrounding a single flat seed.
habitat: Grows in temperate climates. Found in orchards and home gardens in the mid-hills. Prefers well-drained, loamy soil and full sun.
fun_facts: Grows 4–8 m tall. Fruits are 3–6 cm in diameter. Cultivated for over 2,000 years. One of the most adaptable stone fruits. China is the world's largest plum producer.
trivia: Plums are one of the first fruits to ripen in the mid-hills after spring. Their arrival signals the beginning of the summer fruit season. In Japan, plums are used to make umeboshi, a traditional pickled delicacy.

description: The humble potato is the most important vegetable in Nepal, and it's so much more than just a vegetable—it's a staple food. Over 40% of Nepali farmers grow potatoes, and the country produces more than 3.3 million metric tons annually.
fun_facts: Potatoes are the most important non-cereal crop in Nepal.
Nepal has produced over 18 different varieties of potatoes through research.
The crop is a major source of income for farmers, especially in the hills.
trivia: The potato originated in the Andes of South America, where it was domesticated over 7,000 years ago. In Nepal, potatoes are a key ingredient in alu tama, a traditional sour potato curry.

description: The fastest-growing cereal—proso millet matures in just 60-90 days, making it a lifesaver in areas with short growing seasons. In Nepal's mid-hills, it's a traditional crop that's often grown as a rain-fed cereal on marginal lands.
fun_facts: Proso millet is the fastest-growing cereal, maturing in as little as 60 days.
It is highly drought-tolerant and can grow in poor soils.
In Nepal, it's often grown as a secondary crop in the hills.
trivia: In Russia, proso millet is used to make porridge (psheno). In the US, it's primarily grown as birdseed.

The largest of the citrus fruits—pummelo is a relative of the grapefruit, with a thick rind and sweet, mild flesh. In Nepal, it's grown in home gardens and often used as a temple offering. Its segment membranes are very bitter, but the juice vesicles are sweet and refreshing.
identification: A medium-sized evergreen tree reaching 5–10 m with large, winged leaves. The fruit is large, 10–20 cm in diameter, with a thick, greenish-yellow rind and pale pink to yellow flesh.
habitat: Grows in subtropical climates. Found in home gardens and orchards.
fun_facts: Grows 5–10 m tall. Fruits are 10–20 cm in diameter. The largest citrus fruit. Used in temple offerings. Rich in vitamin C.
trivia: Pummelo is one of the original citrus ancestors, along with the citron and mandarin. In Nepal, it's often eaten fresh or used in salads. In Southeast Asia, it's a popular dessert ingredient.

description: A large, trailing vine with edible fruits and young shoots. In Nepal, pumpkin (pharsi) is a staple vegetable, and its tender shoots are also used as greens. It has cooling properties.
identification: A large vine with big, lobed leaves and large, yellow-orange, ribbed fruits.
habitat: Cultivated in temperate and subtropical regions.
fun_facts: Fruits and shoots edible. Has cooling effect. Used as a vegetable.
trivia: Pumpkins are believed to have originated in the Americas and are now grown worldwide. The shoots are a common green in Nepali cuisine.

culinary_uses: Seeds ground into flour; leaves as vegetable
medicinal_uses: Rich in protein and minerals
unique_characters: Ornamental drooping panicles; nutritious
description: A beautiful amaranth with drooping purple flower panicles, grown both as an ornamental and for its nutritious seeds. In Nepal, it's a minor crop but valued for its nutritional content.
fun_facts: Purple amaranth is also known as 'love-lies-bleeding'.
It's native to the Andes and was a staple of the Incas.
It's rich in protein and minerals.
trivia: In South America, purple amaranth is a traditional food.

description: A wild amaranth that grows in the cracks of pavements and the edges of fields, as if determined to survive anywhere. Its leaves have a cooling quality, and its seeds can be used as grain—a food of the Aztecs that still nourishes people today. In Nepal, it's called marshi, a name that echoes across the hills.
identification: An annual herb reaching 0.5–1 m with broad, green or purplish leaves. The young shoots and leaves are the edible portion.
habitat: Grows in tropical and subtropical regions, often in disturbed areas, fields, and along roadsides.
fun_facts: Grows 0.5–1 m tall. Used as a cooling tonic. Seeds can be used as a grain. Found in disturbed areas.
trivia: Amaranth was a staple food of the Aztecs and other Mesoamerican cultures. The seeds are highly nutritious, containing up to 16% protein. In Nepal, it's still gathered wild and eaten as a vegetable.

description: A succulent weed with edible shoots, used as a vegetable. In Nepal, it's called nundhiki and is used for its medicinal properties, including as a febrifuge and antiseptic.
identification: A prostrate, fleshy herb with small, yellow flowers.
habitat: Tropical and subtropical regions, in disturbed areas.
fun_facts: Shoots edible. Rich in omega-3. Used as a febrifuge.
trivia: Purslane is a highly nutritious vegetable, rich in vitamins and omega-3 fatty acids. It's eaten raw or cooked.

A small plant related to taro, with edible leaves. It's found in the Himalayas, and its leaves are used as a vegetable. It's less common than taro but part of the local wild food.
identification: A small herb with heart-shaped leaves.
habitat: Moist, shaded areas in the Himalayas.
fun_facts: Related to taro. Leaves are edible.
trivia: This plant is known for its small size compared to other taro relatives.

description: A thorny shrub with bright red berries, ghangaroo is a common sight in Nepal's hills. The berries are edible but tart, often used to make jams or jellies. It's also planted as an ornamental for its showy fruits.
identification: A thorny evergreen shrub reaching 2–3 m with small, oval leaves and clusters of red berries.
habitat: Grows in temperate forests and scrublands.
fun_facts: A thorny shrub. Berries are edible. Used as an ornamental. Found in the hills.
trivia: In Nepal, the berries of ghangaroo are sometimes used in traditional medicine for digestive issues. The shrub is also a valuable food source for birds.

culinary_uses: Fresh in salads, pickled, cooked in curries
medicinal_uses: Good for digestion; rich in vitamin C
unique_characters: Fast-growing; both root and leaves are edible
description: A crisp, peppery root vegetable that's a winter staple in Nepal. Radishes are eaten fresh in salads, pickled, or cooked in curries. The leaves are also edible and used as a vegetable.
fun_facts: Radishes are fast-growing, maturing in just 30-60 days.
Both the root and the leaves are edible.
They are rich in vitamin C and fiber.
trivia: In Nepal, radishes are often eaten raw with salt and spices. In Japan, radish (daikon) is a staple vegetable.

culinary_uses: Oil for cooking
medicinal_uses: Oil used in massage and traditional remedies
unique_characters: Similar to mustard; used for oil
description: Rapeseed is grown for its oil, which is similar to mustard oil. It's a minor oilseed crop in Nepal, often grown in rotation with wheat and rice.
fun_facts: Rapeseed oil is also known as canola oil (low-erucic acid varieties).
It's a cool-weather crop, grown in winter.
It's an important source of edible oil.
trivia: In Nepal, rapeseed is often used as a cover crop and for green manure.

culinary_uses: Leaves cooked as sag; seeds ground into flour
medicinal_uses: Rich in iron and calcium
unique_characters: Red pigmented variety; ornamental and nutritious
description: A red-pigmented variety of amaranth, grown for both its nutritious seeds and its edible leaves. Rato latte is a traditional crop of Nepal's hills, valued for its vibrant color and nutritional content.
fun_facts: Red amaranth is rich in antioxidants due to its red pigment.
Both the seeds and leaves are edible and nutritious.
It's a registered landrace from Jumla.
trivia: The red pigment in amaranth is a powerful antioxidant.

description: A shrub whose leaves are used as a vegetable, found in the Himalayas.
identification: A shrub with reddish stems and ovate leaves.
fun_facts: Leaves edible.
trivia: This plant is also used for its fiber.

description: The king of Nepali agriculture—rice is more than food, it's life itself. Over half the cultivated land in Nepal is planted with paddy, and it provides more than 50% of the calories we eat. The sight of emerald-green paddies rippling in the Terai breeze is the quintessential image of rural Nepal.
fun_facts: Nepal grows rice at some of the highest elevations in the world—up to 3,000 m in Jumla.
The country has over 3,000 landraces of rice, each adapted to its own microclimate.
In 2021, Nepal produced about 5.6 million metric tons of paddy.
trivia: In Nepal, the rice planting season (ropti) is a time of community celebration, with families helping each other and singing traditional songs called ropti geet. The first rice of the season is often offered to the gods before anyone eats it.

trivia: In Nepal, rice bean is a traditional food of the hill communities.

A wild citrus species, jyamir is a rough lemon found in Nepal's mid-hills. Its fruit is acidic and used as a flavoring, and the tree is often used as a rootstock for other citrus. It's a tough, hardy plant that grows where other citrus might fail.
identification: A small evergreen tree reaching 3–5 m with thorny branches and rough, textured leaves. The fruit is round to oval, 5–8 cm in diameter, with a rough, yellow rind and acidic flesh.
habitat: Grows in subtropical climates, often in forests and along roadsides in the mid-hills.
fun_facts: Grows 3–5 m tall. Fruits are 5–8 cm in diameter. Used as a rootstock. Hardy and resistant. Found in the wild.
trivia: In Nepal, jyamir is sometimes used to make pickles. The tree's ability to withstand harsh conditions makes it a valuable genetic resource for citrus breeding.

A brown-skinned fruit with a grainy sweetness that tastes like caramel and brown sugar. Chikoo is a tropical delight that has adapted well to Nepal's warm pockets. Its flesh is sweet and gritty, a texture that some love and others find strange. In Mexico, it's called sapote, and in Thailand, it's a common fruit. In Nepal, it's a treat found in the lowlands.
identification: An evergreen tree reaching 10–15 m with glossy, elliptical leaves. The fruit is round to oval, 5–10 cm long, with a rough, brown skin. Inside, the flesh is yellow-brown, sweet, and grainy, containing a few shiny black seeds.
habitat: Grows in tropical and subtropical climates. Found in gardens and orchards in the Terai. Prefers well-drained, sandy soil and full sun.
fun_facts: Grows 10–15 m tall. Fruits are 5–10 cm long. Has a caramel-like flavor. Rich in vitamins A and C. The tree produces a latex called chicle, used in chewing gum.
trivia: Sapodilla is the source of chicle, the original base for chewing gum. In Nepal, it's grown in areas like Chitwan and Banke. In the Caribbean, it's often eaten fresh or in milkshakes.

description: A hardy shrub that thrives in the harsh conditions of the high Himalayas. Sea buckthorn produces bright orange berries that are among the most nutrient-dense fruits on Earth. In Nepal, they are harvested by hill communities for traditional medicine. From the mountains of Tibet to the coasts of Europe, sea buckthorn is celebrated for its extraordinary health benefits.
identification: A thorny, deciduous shrub reaching 1–3 m with narrow, silver-green leaves. The fruit is a small, round berry, 4–8 mm in diameter, bright orange to yellow, with a sour, astringent taste.
habitat: Thrives in dry, high-altitude climates. Found in river beds, valleys, and open slopes in the trans-Himalayan region. Prefers well-drained, sandy soil and full sun.
fun_facts: Grows 1–3 m tall. Berries are 4–8 mm in diameter. Contains 200–900 mg of vitamin C per 100 g. Thrives at altitudes up to 4,200 m. Sea buckthorn is native to Europe and Asia and has been used in traditional medicine for centuries.
trivia: Sea buckthorn berries can contain up to 900 mg of vitamin C per 100 g—more than 10 times the amount found in oranges. In Nepal, they are harvested by hill communities for traditional medicine. In Russia, sea buckthorn oil is widely used in cosmetics and traditional remedies.

A seeded banana found in Nepal, used in rituals and sometimes eaten when ripe. The fruits are full of seeds, making them less palatable than seedless bananas, but they have cultural significance. They are often used in religious offerings.
identification: A herbaceous plant with large leaves and seeded banana fruits. The fruit is similar to the wild banana, with many seeds.
habitat: Grows in tropical and subtropical areas, often in gardens and near settlements.
fun_facts: Used in religious offerings. Fruits contain many seeds. Found in Nepal. All season.
trivia: In Nepal, these seeded bananas are sometimes used as a substitute for regular bananas in rituals. They are also fed to livestock.

description: A plant known for its leaves that fold when touched. Its shoots and leaves are used in traditional medicine. In Nepal, it's called lajawati. It's used for glandular swellings and sores.
identification: A creeping herb with fern-like leaves that fold when touched, and pink, fluffy flowers.
habitat: Tropical and subtropical regions, in disturbed areas.
fun_facts: Leaves fold when touched. Used in traditional medicine. Can cause hair loss at high doses.
trivia: Mimosa pudica is a fascinating plant often used in education and research. It also has medicinal uses.

culinary_uses: Oil for cooking; seeds as garnish and in sweets
medicinal_uses: Rich in calcium and healthy fats
unique_characters: Highly drought-tolerant; rich in calcium
cultural_significance: Used in festivals and sweets
description: One of the oldest oilseed crops—sesame is grown for its nutritious seeds and oil. In Nepal, sesame seeds are used in sweets (til ko laddu) and as a garnish. The oil is used for cooking and traditional remedies.
fun_facts: Sesame is one of the oldest oilseed crops, with a history of over 3,000 years.
It's rich in calcium and healthy fats.
The seeds are used in sweets and as a garnish.
trivia: In Nepal, sesame seeds are often used in the festival of Maghe Sankranti (January), when til ko laddu (sesame sweets) are eaten.

description: A common weed that is anything but ordinary—its green and red cultivars are both beautiful and nutritious. In Sri Lanka, it's known as mukunuwenna and sold in markets as a popular leafy green. In Nepal, it grows wild in moist soil, and its young shoots are gathered as bhringi sag, steamed or boiled, a simple meal with deep roots.
identification: A prostrate or creeping herb with opposite, lance-shaped leaves. The young shoots and leaves are the edible portion. The plant has small, white flowers.
habitat: Grows in tropical and subtropical regions, often in moist, disturbed areas, fields, and along roadsides.
fun_facts: Found in tropical and subtropical regions. Has green and red cultivars. Used in traditional medicine. Potential as a functional food.
trivia: This plant is a common weed in many parts of the world, but it is also a valuable vegetable in some cultures. In Sri Lanka, it is known as 'mukunuwenna' and is a popular leafy green. In Ayurvedic medicine, it's used for venereal and neural diseases.

description: A common weed with edible leaves, used as a vegetable. It's also a medicinal plant, used as a haemostatic and diuretic. In Nepal, it grows in disturbed areas and is sometimes gathered.
identification: A small annual herb with rosette leaves and heart-shaped seed pods.
fun_facts: Leaves edible. Used as a haemostatic. Has antifertility properties.
trivia: Shepherd's purse is named for its triangular seed pods, which resemble the purse of a shepherd. It's a well-known weed and a traditional remedy.

A large tree with bright red flowers, whose flowers, fruits, and seeds are used as a vegetable. In Nepal, it's called simal and is used for gastrointestinal issues.
identification: A tall, deciduous tree with large, red flowers and fruits containing cotton-like fibers.
fun_facts: Flowers, fruits, seeds edible. Used for gastrointestinal and skin issues.
trivia: The silk cotton tree is a well-known tree in South Asia, and its cotton is used as a filling for pillows.

One of the most widely distributed amaranths, found in disturbed places across the globe. Its leaves are eaten raw or cooked, and traditional midwives have used it to ease labor pain. In Nepal, it's a humble green that grows wherever the ground is broken, feeding anyone who knows to look.
identification: An annual herb reaching 0.3–0.8 m with smooth, green leaves. The young shoots and leaves are the edible portion.
habitat: Grows in tropical and subtropical regions, often in disturbed areas, fields, and along roadsides.
fun_facts: Grows 0.3–0.8 m tall. Used to reduce labour pain. Eaten raw or cooked. Found in disturbed areas.
trivia: This amaranth is one of the most widely distributed species in its genus and is considered a nutritious leafy vegetable in many parts of the world. It acts as an antirheumatic, analgesic, antiemetic and anti-inflammatory agent.

A fern that's more often admired in gardens than eaten. Its attractive fronds have made it a favorite of houseplant collectors, but in Nepal's forests, it grows wild and unnoticed. Whether it's truly edible remains a mystery—some say yes, but most foragers leave it alone, another of the forest's unresolved secrets.
identification: A medium-sized fern with dark green, divided fronds. The leaves are the edible portion. The plant has a short, creeping rhizome.
habitat: Grows in tropical forests, often in moist, shaded areas. Found in tropical regions worldwide.
fun_facts: Found in tropical regions worldwide. Primarily used as an ornamental. Edibility is uncertain. Grown in gardens and as a houseplant.
trivia: The genus name Tectaria comes from the Latin word 'tectum,' meaning roof, referring to the way the fronds are arranged. This fern is popular among collectors for its attractive foliage in countries like Malaysia and Indonesia.

description: A long, twisted gourd used as a vegetable. In Nepal, it's called ban chichinda and is known for its cathartic and anthelmintic properties.
identification: A climbing vine with long, snake-like, twisted fruits that are green with white stripes.
fun_facts: Fruits edible. Has cathartic properties.
trivia: Snake gourd is a popular vegetable in South Asian and Southeast Asian cuisines. It's often used in curries and stir-fries.

description: The soap berry is a natural source of saponins, used for washing clothes and hair. Its fruits are dried and used as a soap substitute. In Nepal, ritthaa is widely used in rural areas for cleaning.
identification: A medium-sized deciduous tree reaching 10–15 m with compound leaves. The fruit is a small, round drupe, 1–2 cm in diameter, with a brown, leathery skin and a single seed.
habitat: Grows in subtropical and tropical areas, often in forests and along roadsides.
fun_facts: Grows 10–15 m tall. Fruits are 1–2 cm in diameter. Used as a natural soap. Found in Nepal.
trivia: The soap berry is a traditional detergent in Nepal. The oil extracted from its seeds is used for making soap and bio-lubricants. The tree is also valued for its timber.

culinary_uses: Ground into flour for flatbreads and porridge
medicinal_uses: Good source of iron and B vitamins
unique_characters: Highly drought-tolerant; grows in hot, dry areas
description: The drought-defying giant—sorghum is a tall, sturdy grain that thrives in the hot, dry conditions of the Terai where other cereals struggle. The grain is ground into flour and used to make flatbreads and porridge.
fun_facts: Sorghum is the fifth most important cereal crop in the world.
It is highly drought-tolerant and can grow in areas with as little as 400 mm of annual rainfall.
In Nepal, it's grown on a small scale in the Terai.
trivia: In Africa, sorghum is a staple food, used to make porridge, flatbreads, and beer.

description: A developed variety of sour orange from indigenous genetic resources. It's likely used as a rootstock or for its essential oils.
identification: A citrus tree with sour fruits.
fun_facts: A developed variety from indigenous resources.
trivia: Sour oranges are often used in marmalades and as rootstocks. This variety is part of Nepal's citrus breeding program.

description: A common weed with edible leaves, used as a vegetable. In traditional medicine, it's used for stomachache, hepatitis, and inflammation. In Nepal, it's called dudhikanda.
identification: A herb with lobed leaves and yellow flowers, with a milky sap.
habitat: Temperate and subtropical regions, in disturbed areas.
fun_facts: Leaves edible. Used for stomachache and hepatitis.
trivia: Sow thistle is a wild green that has been used as food and medicine for centuries. It's a relative of the cultivated lettuce.

primary_use: Edible oil, food (tofu, soy milk), animal feed
culinary_uses: Used to make tofu, soy milk, tempeh; cooked as vegetable
medicinal_uses: Rich in protein, isoflavones, and omega-3 fatty acids
unique_characters: High protein content; nitrogen-fixing; source of isoflavones
economic_importance: Growing cash crop; used for oil and food products
description: The miracle bean—soybean is one of the most versatile and nutritious crops on the planet. In Nepal, it's grown as a pulse and oilseed, and its products (tofu, soy milk) are gaining popularity.
fun_facts: Soybean is one of the most protein-rich plant sources.
It's the main ingredient in tofu, soy milk, and tempeh.
The crop is nitrogen-fixing, improving soil fertility.
trivia: Soybean has been cultivated in East Asia for over 3,000 years. In Nepal, it's often grown as an intercrop with maize.

description: A fragrant herb used as a culinary flavoring. In Nepal, pudina is widely used in chutneys, teas, and curries. It has cooling and digestive properties.
identification: A creeping perennial herb with square stems, opposite, serrated leaves, and spikes of purple flowers.
habitat: Cultivated in temperate and subtropical regions.
fun_facts: Leaves edible and aromatic. Used for digestive issues. Cooling effect.
trivia: Spearmint is one of the oldest culinary herbs, used in ancient Greek and Roman cuisine. It's a common garden herb in Nepal.

culinary_uses: Cooked as sag, fresh in salads
medicinal_uses: Rich in iron, calcium, and vitamins A, C, K, and folate
description: The green powerhouse—spinach is one of the most nutritious leafy vegetables. In Nepal, it's eaten as sag (cooked green) and used in curries. The rich iron and vitamin content make it a favorite for health-conscious families.
fun_facts: Spinach is native to Persia (Iran) and was introduced to Nepal through trade.
It's rich in iron, calcium, and vitamins.
The famous cartoon character Popeye made spinach famous for its iron content.
trivia: In Nepal, spinach is often cooked with garlic, ginger, and spices to make a delicious sag.

description: A plant that defends itself with spines but gives generously to those who know how to handle it. Its young shoots are edible and its medicinal uses are many—but caution: it can induce abortion, a fact that has made it both feared and respected. In Nepal, it grows wild, a survivor in fields and roadsides.
identification: An annual herb reaching 0.5–1 m with spines at the leaf axils. The young shoots and leaves are the edible portion.
habitat: Grows in tropical and subtropical regions, often in disturbed areas, fields, and along roadsides.
fun_facts: Grows 0.5–1 m tall. Has spines at leaf axils. Used in traditional medicine. Used in Ayurveda for fevers.
trivia: Caution: This plant can induce abortion, so it should not be consumed by pregnant women. The spines make it easy to identify, and it's often used as a green manure. In Ayurveda, it's used as a febrifuge, antipyretic, laxative and diuretic.

description: A pungent herb with a flavor that's like cilantro but stronger—it's called 'culantro' in the Caribbean and is a favorite in Asian cuisines. Its leaves are used in curries and rice, and it's valued for its medicinal properties. In Nepal, it grows in the hills, a taste of the tropics in the cool mountains.
identification: A biennial herb reaching 0.3–0.6 m with long, toothed leaves with spiny margins. The leaves are the primary edible portion.
habitat: Grows in tropical and subtropical regions. Found in gardens and along roadsides.
fun_facts: Grows 0.3–0.6 m tall. Used as a coriander substitute. Found in tropical regions. Popular in Caribbean and Asian cuisines.
trivia: This plant is often confused with cilantro (Coriandrum sativum) but has a stronger, more pungent flavor. In some regions, it is used as a remedy for colds and flu. In Nepal, it's a lesser-known herb but is gaining popularity.

description: A wild relative of bitter gourd, with spiny fruits. Its fruits are used as a vegetable and have medicinal properties, including anti-diabetic and anti-inflammatory effects. In Nepal, it's called ban karela.
identification: A vine with spiny fruits similar to bitter gourd but smaller.
fun_facts: Fruits edible. Used for hypertension. Has anti-diabetic properties.
trivia: This plant is also known as 'kakora' in some parts of India and is used like bitter gourd.

A plant whose leaves are used as a vegetable. In Ayurveda, it's known as punarva and is used for liver and joint pain. In Nepal, it's called punarva.
identification: A creeping herb with opposite, fleshy leaves and small, pinkish flowers.
habitat: Tropical and subtropical regions, in disturbed areas.
fun_facts: Leaves edible. Used for liver and joint pain. Has antiaging properties.
trivia: Boerhavia diffusa is a well-known Ayurvedic herb used for its rejuvenating properties.

description: With its spore stalk standing taller than its leaf, this fern is hard to miss once you know what to look for. It's a plant that has made its way into traditional medicine across Asia—the whole plant is used to clear heat and promote circulation, a belief that has persisted for generations.
identification: A small fern with a single, simple leaf blade and a separate spore-bearing stalk. The plant grows 5–20 cm tall. The young fronds are the edible portion.
habitat: Grows in tropical and subtropical regions, often in grasslands, open forests, and disturbed areas.
fun_facts: Grows 5–20 cm tall. Found in tropical and subtropical regions. Harvested from February to April. Used in traditional medicine.
trivia: The spore-bearing stalk of this fern can be up to twice as long as the leaf blade, making it easily distinguishable from other adder's tongue ferns. In Chinese traditional medicine, similar ferns are used for similar purposes.

identification: A tall herb with stinging hairs, serrated leaves.
habitat: Temperate regions, in moist, nutrient-rich soils.
fun_facts: Leaves edible after cooking. Rich in iron. Used for cold.
trivia: Stinging nettle is a nutritious wild green and is used in soups and teas. The sting disappears when cooked.

description: A bright, fragrant berry that has become increasingly popular in Nepal's mid-hills. Strawberries are a modern success story, grown in cool climates for fresh eating and processing. Strawberry farming has become a successful commercial venture near Kathmandu and Pokhara. From the farms of California to the greenhouses of Europe, strawberries are one of the world's most beloved fruits.
identification: A low-growing, herbaceous perennial plant with trifoliate leaves and runners that spread across the ground. The fruit is small, 1–3 cm in diameter, with bright red skin covered in tiny seeds, and sweet, aromatic, juicy red flesh.
habitat: Thrives in temperate climates. Found in farms and gardens in the Kathmandu Valley and mid-hills. Prefers well-drained, loamy soil and full sun.
fun_facts: Grows 10–30 cm tall. Fruits are 1–3 cm in diameter. Ready to harvest in 2–3 months. A relatively new crop in Nepal. The United States is the world's largest strawberry producer.
trivia: Strawberries are not berries botanically—they're aggregate fruits. In Nepal, strawberry farming is a successful commercial venture near Kathmandu and Pokhara. In France, strawberries are traditionally served with cream and sugar.

culinary_uses: Juice as drink; sugar and jaggery as sweeteners
medicinal_uses: Juice for energy; rich in antioxidants
economic_importance: Major cash crop in the Terai
description: The sweet giant of Nepal's Terai—sugarcane is a major cash crop that provides sugar, jaggery, and molasses. The tall, green canes sway in the Terai breeze, and the fresh juice is a popular drink.
fun_facts: Sugarcane was first domesticated in Southeast Asia over 10,000 years ago.
Nepal produces over 3 million metric tons of sugarcane annually.
Fresh sugarcane juice is a popular drink in the Terai.
trivia: In Nepal, sugarcane is often sold fresh on the streets, where people chew it to extract the sweet juice.

culinary_uses: Oil for cooking; roasted seeds as snack
medicinal_uses: Oil rich in vitamin E
unique_characters: Large flower heads; high oil content
description: A new oilseed crop gaining popularity in Nepal—sunflower is grown for its edible oil and seeds. The oil is light and healthy, rich in vitamin E. The roasted seeds are a popular snack.
fun_facts: Sunflower is native to North America and was domesticated over 3,000 years ago.
The oil is rich in vitamin E and healthy fats.
The seeds are a popular snack.
trivia: Sunflowers are known for heliotropism—the flower heads follow the sun during the day.

description: Chaksi is a sweet lime found in Nepal's mid-hills. Unlike regular limes, it's low in acidity and has a mild, sweet flavor. It's often eaten fresh or juiced, and its fragrant zest is used in perfumes and flavorings. A refreshing fruit for the autumn season.
identification: A small evergreen tree reaching 3–5 m with oval, glossy leaves. The fruit is round to oval, 5–8 cm in diameter, with a greenish-yellow rind and sweet, low-acid flesh.
habitat: Grows in subtropical climates, often in home gardens and orchards in the mid-hills.
fun_facts: Grows 3–5 m tall. Fruits are 5–8 cm in diameter. Low acidity, sweet flavor. Used for juice and fragrance. Rich in vitamin C.
trivia: In Nepal, sweet lime is often eaten with a sprinkle of salt and chili powder. It's a popular snack during the winter months. The fruit is also used in traditional medicine for coughs.

description: A tuberous root vegetable, sweet potato is a staple in many parts of the world. In Nepal, it's called sakharkand and is eaten boiled, roasted, or in curries. Its leaves are also edible.
identification: A creeping vine with heart-shaped leaves and large, starchy, sweet-tasting tubers.
habitat: Cultivated in tropical and subtropical regions.
fun_facts: Tubers edible and sweet. Leaves also edible. Rich in vitamins.
trivia: Sweet potatoes are not related to true potatoes. They are a major food crop in many developing countries and are rich in beta-carotene.

culinary_uses: Boiled, roasted, fried, curried
medicinal_uses: Rich in beta-carotene and vitamin A
unique_characters: Rich in beta-carotene; drought-tolerant
description: A nutritious tuber with a sweet taste—sweet potato is a popular vegetable in Nepal's Terai. It's rich in beta-carotene (vitamin A) and is eaten boiled, roasted, or curried.
fun_facts: Sweet potatoes are not related to potatoes—they're in the morning glory family.
They are rich in beta-carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A.
They are drought-tolerant and grow well in sandy soils.
trivia: In Nepal, sweet potatoes are often roasted in their skins. In the US, sweet potatoes are a traditional Thanksgiving dish.

uses: Chutneys, curries, drinks, traditional remedies, confectionery, preserves, sherbets
description: A sour, tangy fruit that adds distinctive flavor to South Asian cuisine. Tamarind is one of the most important culinary fruits in Nepal's Terai, used in everything from chutneys to cooling drinks. From Mexico to Thailand, tamarind has become an essential ingredient in kitchens worldwide.
identification: A large evergreen tree reaching 12–30 m with feathery, compound leaves. The fruit is a pod, 5–15 cm long, brown, with a brittle shell containing a sour, sticky pulp and several seeds.
habitat: Grows in tropical climates. Found in Terai gardens, orchards, and along roadsides. Prefers well-drained, sandy soil and full sun.
fun_facts: Grows 12–30 m tall. Pods are 5–15 cm long. Cultivated for thousands of years. Rich in minerals and antioxidants. Tamarind is native to tropical Africa but has been naturalized in Asia and the Americas.
trivia: Tamarind is often called the 'date of India.' In Nepal, a refreshing drink made from tamarind pulp is a popular summer beverage. In Mexico, tamarind is used to make sweet and spicy candies.

culinary_uses: Fresh, in juice
medicinal_uses: Rich in vitamin C
description: A type of mandarin with a sweet, tangy flavor, enjoyed fresh in Nepal's hills.
fun_facts: Tangerines are a type of mandarin.
They are rich in vitamin C.
The fruit is eaten fresh.
trivia: In Nepal, tangerines are often eaten fresh as a snack.

Taro is a staple root vegetable in many parts of the world. In Nepal, its tubers are boiled, roasted, or curried, and its leaves are also used as a vegetable. The plant is rich in starch and nutrients, but must be cooked to remove acridity.
identification: A herbaceous plant with large, heart-shaped leaves and underground corms (tubers). The tubers and leaves are the edible portions.
habitat: Grows in moist, tropical and subtropical areas, often in wetlands.
fun_facts: Grows in wetlands. Tubers are starch-rich. Leaves used as vegetable. Cultivated worldwide.
trivia: Taro is one of the oldest cultivated crops, with a history of over 10,000 years. In Nepal, it's a common food in the hills and Terai.

culinary_uses: Boiled, fried, curried; leaves as vegetable
medicinal_uses: Good for digestive health
unique_characters: Contains calcium oxalate (must be cooked to remove)
description: A tropical plant with edible corms and leaves. Taro is a popular vegetable in Nepal, where the corms are used in curries and the leaves are cooked as sag. It must be cooked properly to remove calcium oxalate crystals.
fun_facts: Taro was one of the first domesticated crops in Asia.
Both the corms and leaves are edible.
It contains calcium oxalate, which must be removed by cooking.
trivia: In Nepal, taro leaves (pinde ko sag) are a popular green vegetable, often cooked with meat or spices.

soil_type: Well-drained, acidic, rich in organic matter
culinary_uses: Fermented, dried, and brewed as tea
medicinal_uses: Rich in antioxidants; good for heart health
economic_importance: Major cash crop in the eastern hills
description: The fragrant leaf that's the soul of Nepali hospitality—tea (chiya) is grown in the beautiful hills of eastern Nepal. The lush tea gardens of Ilam produce some of the finest tea in the world.
fun_facts: Tea is one of the most popular beverages in the world.
Nepal produces both black and green tea.
The eastern hills of Nepal are famous for their tea gardens.
trivia: In Nepal, tea (chiya) is often served with milk and sugar in the morning and evening.

description: Barro is one of the three fruits in the Ayurvedic formula Triphala. Its fruits are edible but astringent, often used for medicinal purposes rather than eaten fresh. It's a large tree found in Nepal's forests.
identification: A large deciduous tree reaching 15–30 m with broad, oval leaves. The fruit is a drupe, 2–3 cm long, greenish-yellow, with a hard stone and fibrous pulp.
habitat: Grows in tropical and subtropical forests.
fun_facts: Grows 15–30 m tall. Fruits are 2–3 cm long. Used in Triphala. Found in Nepal.
trivia: In Ayurveda, barro is used to treat digestive disorders and respiratory conditions. The fruit is also used in traditional medicine in Nepal.

description: Harro is another Triphala fruit, known as the 'king of medicines' in Ayurveda. Its fruits are used for their strong laxative and digestive properties. In Nepal, it's a common medicinal plant, often found in forests and near temples.
identification: A medium-sized deciduous tree reaching 10–20 m with oval, pointed leaves. The fruit is a drupe, 2–3 cm long, yellowish-brown, with a wrinkled skin and astringent pulp.
habitat: Grows in tropical and subtropical forests.
fun_facts: Grows 10–20 m tall. Fruits are 2–3 cm long. Known as the 'king of medicines.' Used in Triphala. Found in Nepal.
trivia: Harro is a staple in Ayurvedic medicine, used for everything from constipation to detoxification. In Nepal, it's often collected from wild trees and sold in markets.

description: A poisonous plant with medicinal uses—thorn apple is used in small doses for asthma and insomnia. Its seeds yield an oil used for hair growth. It's a plant that demands respect and caution.
identification: An annual herb reaching 1–1.5 m with large, toothed leaves and trumpet-shaped white flowers. The fruit is a spiny capsule containing many seeds.
habitat: Grows in tropical and subtropical areas, often in waste lands and along roadsides.
fun_facts: Grows 1–1.5 m tall. Has trumpet-shaped flowers. Used in medicine. Toxic if misused.
trivia: Datura is a powerful hallucinogen and has been used in religious ceremonies in some cultures. In Nepal, it's used cautiously in traditional medicine. The plant is also known as 'devil's trumpet.'

medicinal_uses: Limited medicinal use (with caution)
unique_characters: Contains nicotine (addictive alkaloid); high-value cash crop
economic_importance: Cash crop in some areas
description: A controversial but important cash crop—tobacco is grown in the Terai for its dried leaves, which are used for smoking and chewing. It's a high-value crop, but its use is declining due to health concerns.
fun_facts: Tobacco was first cultivated in South America over 5,000 years ago.
It's a high-value cash crop in some areas.
The leaves are dried and processed for smoking or chewing.
trivia: In Nepal, tobacco is sometimes used in traditional medicine, but with caution due to its addictive and harmful effects.

culinary_uses: Fresh in salads, cooked in curries, made into sauce
medicinal_uses: Rich in vitamin C and lycopene (antioxidant)
economic_importance: Major vegetable crop
description: The vibrant red fruit that's the soul of Nepali curries and chutneys—tomato is one of the most beloved vegetables in Nepal. From simple curries to spicy chutneys, golbheda is an essential part of Nepali cuisine.
fun_facts: Tomatoes are technically fruits (berries), but are used as vegetables.
They are rich in lycopene, an antioxidant that is better absorbed when cooked.
Nepal produces several varieties adapted to different altitudes.
trivia: In Nepal, tomato chutney is a popular condiment, often eaten with dhindo and roti.

description: The national flower of Nepal, its flowers are used as a vegetable and in traditional medicine. In Nepal, it's called laligurans. The flowers are used to make juice and also dried for diarrhea.
identification: A small tree with leathery leaves and clusters of red or pink trumpet-shaped flowers.
fun_facts: Flowers edible. Used as a refresher. National flower.
trivia: Rhododendron arboreum is a symbol of Nepal and its flowers are used in traditional remedies for high altitude sickness.

culinary_uses: Fresh or dried in curries; used as a spice and dye
medicinal_uses: Anti-inflammatory; good for digestion and skin health
unique_characters: Contains curcumin (active compound with anti-inflammatory properties)
cultural_significance: Essential in Nepali cooking and traditional medicine; used in religious ceremonies
description: The golden spice of Nepal—turmeric (besar) is essential in Nepali cooking and traditional medicine. The bright yellow rhizome adds color and flavor to curries and is prized for its anti-inflammatory properties.
fun_facts: Turmeric has been used in South Asia for over 4,000 years.
The active compound curcumin has powerful anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties.
Nepal produces several varieties of turmeric.
trivia: In Nepal, turmeric is also used in religious ceremonies and as a dye for clothing.

culinary_uses: Cooked in curries, pickled, eaten raw in salads, leaves as sag
medicinal_uses: Good source of vitamin C and fiber
description: A cool-season root vegetable with a sweet, mild flavor. Turnips are used in curries, pickles, and salads. The leaves are also used as a green vegetable (salagam ko sag).
fun_facts: Turnips are a cool-season crop that grows best in the hills.
Both the root and leaves are edible.
They are rich in vitamin C and fiber.
trivia: In Nepal, turnips are often pickled (salgam ko achar) and served with meals.

culinary_uses: Cooked in curries, pickled, fresh in salads
medicinal_uses: Rich in vitamin C and fiber
unique_characters: Both root and leaves are edible; cool-weather crop
description: A cool-weather root vegetable that's a winter favorite in Nepal. Turnips are cooked in curries, pickled, or eaten fresh. The leaves are also edible and used as a vegetable.
fun_facts: Turnips are a cool-weather crop, grown in winter.
Both the root and the leaves are edible.
They are rich in vitamin C and fiber.
trivia: In Nepal, turnips are often pickled (saljam ko achar). In Europe, turnips are a traditional winter vegetable.
