In the cool, shaded corners of Nepal's forests, the young fronds of this fern unfurl like green scrolls, ready to be gathered. The locals call it neuro, and they know exactly when to find it—just as the rains begin to whisper through the leaves. The tender shoots are a seasonal delight, stir-fried with garlic and a pinch of salt, their subtle flavor a taste of the forest itself.
identification: A medium-sized fern with delicate, divided fronds. The young, unfurled fronds (fiddleheads) are the edible portion. The plant has a creeping rhizome and grows in moist, shaded areas. Fronds can grow 30–100 cm long.
habitat: Grows in tropical and subtropical forests, often in moist, shaded areas along streams and forest floors at elevations up to 2,100 m.
fun_facts: Ferns are one of the oldest plant groups on Earth, with fossils dating back over 350 million years. Rich in dietary fiber and minerals. In Japan, fiddlehead ferns are a seasonal delicacy called 'zenmai.'
trivia: In Nepal, fiddlehead ferns are a seasonal delicacy that connects people to the forest. In many cultures worldwide, ferns have been used for food and medicine since ancient times.

description: Another member of the fern family, kaloneura is a humble forest vegetable that many Nepali families still gather from the wild. Its young fronds are a reminder of simpler times, when the forest provided daily sustenance and every leaf had a name known to the elders.
identification: A medium-sized fern with divided fronds. The young, unfurled fronds are the edible portion. The plant grows from a creeping rhizome.
habitat: Grows in moist, shaded areas in forests and along streams in the Himalayan region.
fun_facts: Belongs to the same family as the popular vegetable fern. Found in the Himalayan region. Young fronds are harvested in May-June.
trivia: Like many edible ferns, the young fronds must be harvested before they unfurl completely for the best texture and flavor. In neighboring Bhutan, similar ferns are also collected and eaten.

description: A fern whose taxonomic identity is still debated—but that doesn't stop people from eating it. The young stems of this fern are occasionally gathered, though it's less known than its relatives. Like many wild foods, it's a disappearing knowledge, remembered only by the oldest foragers.
identification: A fern with large, divided fronds. The young shoots are the edible portion. The plant has a creeping rhizome.
habitat: Grows in moist, shaded areas in forests. Found in tropical and subtropical regions.
fun_facts: Taxonomic status is currently unresolved. Related species in East Asia are known to be edible. Found in tropical regions.
trivia: The genus Woodwardia is named after English botanist Thomas Jenkinson Woodward. In East Asia, related species are sometimes harvested for food and medicine.

description: A graceful fern that creeps through Himalayan forests, forming loose clusters of fronds. Its young leaves are both cooked fresh and preserved in pickles—a tradition that keeps the taste of the hills alive through the long winter. It's found at elevations from subtropical to alpine zones.
identification: A medium-sized fern with bright green, divided fronds. The young, unfurled fronds are the edible portion. The plant spreads through a creeping rhizome.
habitat: Grows in moist, shaded areas in forests, often along streams and in gullies at elevations from 400–3,300 m in the Himalayas.
fun_facts: Found at elevations from 400–3,300 m. Forms loose clusters through creeping rhizomes. Used both fresh and pickled. Found throughout the Himalayan region.
trivia: This fern is one of the few edible ferns that can be found at such a wide range of elevations. In Himalayan regions, pickling ferns is a traditional way of preserving them for winter.

description: Known by several names across Nepal, this fern is valued both as food and medicine. Traditional healers use it to purify the blood and ease muscle pain—a remedy that has been trusted for generations. But there's a caution: it contains a toxic compound, so like so many wild foods, moderation is key.
identification: A medium-sized fern with dark green, divided fronds. The young, unfurled fronds are the edible portion. The plant has a short, creeping rhizome.
habitat: Grows in moist, shaded areas in forests, often along streams and in gullies in the Himalayan region.
fun_facts: Contains ptaquiloside, a toxic compound. Used in traditional medicine for pain relief. Harvested from March to May. Common in Nepal.
trivia: The compound ptaquiloside found in this fern is also present in bracken fern, but in lower concentrations. Traditional preparation methods such as boiling and changing the water may help reduce toxicity.

description: A Himalayan fern that has been gathered for generations, though always with care. Its young fronds contain the same compounds that make bracken dangerous, but the elders know how to prepare it safely—soaking and boiling, then discarding the water, a ritual repeated until the toxins are gone.
identification: A medium-sized fern with dark green, divided fronds. The young, unfurled fronds are the edible portion. The plant has a short, creeping rhizome.
habitat: Grows in moist, shaded areas in forests in the Himalayan region.
fun_facts: Contains ptaquiloside, a toxic compound. Found in the Himalayan region. Harvested in May-June. Related to the wood fern family.
trivia: Like other ferns containing ptaquiloside, traditional preparation methods such as boiling and changing the water may help reduce toxicity. Similar practices are found across Asia for preparing toxic wild foods.

description: An edible fern with a hidden power—its leaves contain a protein that's toxic to whiteflies. This discovery has led to the development of insect-resistant cotton, a remarkable journey from a Himalayan fern to a high-tech crop. In Nepal, it's still used simply as a vegetable, a salad green, and a remedy for stomach troubles.
identification: A medium-sized fern with dark green, divided fronds. The young shoots are the edible portion. The plant has a short, creeping rhizome.
habitat: Grows in tropical forests, often in moist, shaded areas. Found in Asia.
fun_facts: Has insecticidal properties. Used in salads and for gastric issues. Contains insecticidal protein. Found in Asia.
trivia: The insecticidal protein from this fern, called Tma12, has been used to develop genetically modified cotton that is resistant to whiteflies, offering an environmentally friendly alternative to chemical pesticides. It's a remarkable example of a wild plant solving a modern agricultural problem.

description: A shield fern whose shoots are gathered in the same way foragers have done for generations. Its relatives across the genus are known to be edible, a shared knowledge that extends across tropical regions. In the quiet of the Himalayan spring, the same practice continues—young shoots harvested before they unfurl.
identification: A medium-sized fern with divided fronds. The young shoots are the edible portion. The plant has a short, creeping rhizome.
habitat: Grows in tropical and subtropical forests, often in moist, shaded areas.
fun_facts: Belongs to the Thelypteridaceae family. Related species are edible. Found in tropical and subtropical regions. Harvested in spring.
trivia: The genus Cyclosorus includes many species that are commonly known as 'shield ferns' due to the shape of their fronds. In Hawaii, related species are used in traditional practices.

description: In Nepal, the tender fronds of this fern are cooked and eaten, while the stipes—the stalks—are woven into handicrafts. It's a plant that serves two purposes: food and craft, a reminder that the forest provides in many ways. In neighboring countries, similar ferns are used for both.
identification: A medium-sized fern with divided fronds. The tender fronds are the edible portion. The plant has a short, creeping rhizome.
habitat: Grows in tropical and subtropical forests, often in moist, shaded areas. Found in Asia.
fun_facts: Found in Asia. Used in handicrafts. Harvested in June-July. Known in Nepal and other parts of Asia.
trivia: The stipes (stalks) of this fern are strong and flexible, making them suitable for weaving and other handicraft uses. In Southeast Asia, similar ferns are used for making mats and baskets.

description: A plant with bitter leaves and orange-red flowers that brighten the forest edge. In some communities, those bitter leaves become chutneys, their sharp taste balanced with salt and chili. The flowers are eaten as a vegetable, and the whole plant is used for coughs and colds—a bitter medicine for a common ailment.
identification: A shrub or small tree with opposite, elliptical leaves and clusters of tubular flowers. The flowers are typically orange-red. The flowers and leaves are the edible portions.
habitat: Grows in tropical and subtropical regions, often in gardens and along roadsides. Found in Asia.
fun_facts: Found in Asia. Used in traditional medicine. Flowers eaten as a vegetable. Harvested from March-May.
trivia: The bitter taste of the leaves is valued in some traditional cuisines, where bitterness is believed to have medicinal properties and aid digestion. Similar practices exist in India and Southeast Asia.

description: In the shallow waters of tropical ponds, this aquatic herb grows with its arrow-shaped leaves rising above the surface. Its starchy rhizomes can be ground into flour or boiled into soups—food that sustained people through lean times. In many countries, it's also used as green manure, feeding the soil that feeds the people.
identification: An aquatic herb with arrowhead-shaped leaves and a creeping rhizome. The rhizomes are the primary edible portion. The plant produces small, white flowers.
habitat: Grows in shallow water, ponds, ditches, and rice paddies. Found in tropical and subtropical regions.
fun_facts: Found in tropical regions. Used as a green manure. Rhizomes can be made into flour. Grows in shallow water.
trivia: The rhizomes of this plant are rich in starch and have been used as a food source in many tropical regions. In some areas, it is cultivated in rice paddies as a companion crop. Similar aquatic plants are eaten in Southeast Asia and Africa.

description: A plant whose flowers are so striking they're used in dried bouquets—but its leaves are also good eating. In Nepal, the young leaves are cooked as a vegetable, while the flowers provide medicine and beauty. It's a plant that feeds, heals, and decorates, a triple gift from the garden.
identification: An annual herb reaching 0.5–1 m with broad leaves and distinctive, feathery flower spikes in various colors. The young leaves are the edible portion.
habitat: Grows in tropical and subtropical regions. Cultivated as a vegetable and ornamental.
fun_facts: Grows 0.5–1 m tall. Used as a diuretic. Grown as an ornamental. Harvested from August to December.
trivia: The flowers of this plant are often used in dried flower arrangements because they retain their color and shape for a long time. In some cultures, the flowers are used in traditional medicine. In Nepal, it's sometimes grown in gardens for its ornamental value and edible leaves.

description: A shrub that sometimes grows as a herb, with colorful fruits that are popular with birds and beautiful to the eye. Its leaves and shoots are eaten as vegetables, and traditional healers use it for sores. In gardens, it's grown for its ornamental value as much as its food.
identification: A shrub or herb reaching 1–2 m with ovate leaves and colorful fruits. The leaves and shoots are the edible portion.
habitat: Grows in tropical and subtropical regions, often in forests and along roadsides.
fun_facts: Grows 1–2 m tall. Used in traditional medicine. Grown as an ornamental. Found in tropical and subtropical regions.
trivia: The colorful fruits of this plant are popular with birds, which help to disperse its seeds. The plant is sometimes confused with true amaranths but belongs to a different genus. In Australia, related species are used in indigenous bush foods.

description: A wild onion that grows in the high Himalayas, where the air is thin and the winters are long. Its garlicky flavor has made it a prized spice and vegetable for mountain communities. The bulbs and leaves are gathered in summer, dried, and stored for the cold months—a precious green in a land of scarcity.
identification: A perennial herb with onion-like leaves and bulbs. The leaves and bulbs are the edible portions.
habitat: Grows in temperate and alpine regions of the Himalayas. Found in meadows and rocky slopes.
fun_facts: Found in the Himalayas. Used as a digestive. Has a garlicky flavor. Harvested in July-August.
trivia: This wild onion is well-adapted to high-altitude environments and can survive harsh winters. Its leaves emerge early in spring and are often one of the first green plants available. It's a vital source of flavor and nutrition in mountain communities.

description: Another wild onion from the Himalayan slopes, where it's valued for its mild flavor and medicinal properties. Its leaves are used to season dishes, and traditional healers use it to treat wounds and purify the blood. In the high mountains, it's one of the few sources of fresh greenery in the late autumn.
identification: A perennial herb with onion-like leaves and bulbs. The leaves are the primary edible portion.
habitat: Grows in temperate regions of the Himalayas. Found in meadows and rocky slopes.
fun_facts: Found in the Himalayas. Used in traditional medicine. Has a mild onion flavor. Harvested in October-November.
trivia: This wild onion is known for its ability to thrive in the harsh conditions of the high Himalayas, where it is often one of the few edible greens available during certain seasons. It's used in local cuisine and traditional medicine.

description: A wild allium that tastes like green garlic, growing in the high Himalayas where few other plants dare. It's used as a vegetable and seasoning, a green flush of flavor in a landscape of stone and ice. Named after a German explorer, it's a reminder of the many travelers who have been captivated by the plants of the Himalayas.
identification: A perennial herb with onion-like leaves and bulbs. The leaves are the primary edible portion.
habitat: Grows in alpine regions of the Himalayas. Found in meadows and rocky slopes.
fun_facts: Found in the Himalayas. Tastes like green garlic. Used as a vegetable. Found at high altitudes.
trivia: The plant was described by the British botanist Charles Henry Wright in the late 19th century and is named after the German explorer and naturalist Wilhelm von Pratti. In local cuisine, it's used fresh or dried.

description: A wild onion that bears the name of the British botanist who collected it—Richard Strachey, who traveled the Himalayas in the 19th century. Its leaves have a distinctive onion flavor and are used as a spice and vegetable. It's a plant that has been feeding mountain communities for longer than anyone can remember.
identification: A perennial herb with onion-like leaves and bulbs. The leaves are the primary edible portion.
habitat: Grows in temperate regions of the Himalayas. Found in meadows and rocky slopes.
fun_facts: Found in the Himalayas. Used as a spice. Has a distinctive onion flavor. Harvested in August-October.
trivia: This wild onion is named after the British botanist Richard Strachey, who collected plants in the Himalayas during the 19th century. It's still used in local cuisine and traditional medicine.

description: A tree whose young shoots and fruits are both edible, though it's the wood that is most famous—used in traditional medicine for wounds and heart health. In Nepal, it's a lesser-known species, but across Asia, its fruits are valued as a food source. The powder from its wood is applied to cuts, a healing tradition that has persisted for centuries.
identification: A medium-sized tree reaching 10–15 m with compound leaves and small, round fruits. The young shoots and fruits are the edible portions.
habitat: Grows in tropical and subtropical forests. Found in Asia.
fun_facts: Grows 10–15 m tall. Used as a cardiotonic. Found in Asia. Harvested in May-June.
trivia: The fruits of this tree are sometimes called 'charoli' and are used in traditional Indian cuisine. The wood is also used for making furniture and tools. In Nepal, it's a valuable tree for both timber and food.

description: A low-growing plant from the parsley family, found in the meadows of the Himalayas. Its name means 'ghost's hair,' a reference to its mysterious appearance. It's one of the lesser-known edible plants, part of a family famous for its aromatic herbs—carrots, celery, and dill are its cousins.
identification: A herbaceous plant with divided leaves. The leaves are the primary edible portion.
habitat: Grows in temperate regions. Found in meadows and grasslands.
fun_facts: Found in temperate regions. Used as a vegetable. Harvested in July-August. Belongs to the Apiaceae family.
trivia: This plant is named after its characteristic low, depressed growth form. It is one of the many lesser-known edible plants in the Himalayan region. In Bhutan, similar species are used in local cuisine.

description: A relative of water celery, growing in the same wet habitats. Its leaves are aromatic and used as a seasoning, a delicate flavor in a landscape of bold spices. It's a lesser-known herb, but in some parts of Nepal, it's still gathered and used in traditional dishes.
identification: A herbaceous plant with hollow stems and divided leaves. The leaves are the primary edible portion.
habitat: Grows in wet areas, along stream banks, and in marshes.
fun_facts: Used for flavoring. Related to water celery. Found in wet areas. Harvested in May-June.
trivia: This species of water celery is less well-known than Oenanthe javanica but is used similarly as a flavouring herb in some traditional dishes. In Nepal, it's a wild plant of wetland edges.

description: A high-altitude plant from the parsley family, found in the rocky meadows of the Himalayas. Its leaves are used as a vegetable and a remedy for stomach troubles. In the thin air of the mountains, even a small green leaf is a precious source of sustenance.
identification: A herbaceous plant with divided leaves. The leaves are the primary edible portion.
habitat: Grows at high altitudes in the Himalayas. Found in meadows and rocky slopes.
fun_facts: Found in the Himalayas. Used for dysentery. Harvested in July-August. Found at high altitudes.
trivia: This plant is part of the Pleurospermum genus, which includes many species that grow in the high Himalayas. Some are used in traditional medicine for various ailments. In Nepal, it's a wild vegetable of the mountains.

description: A lesser-known member of the parsley family, growing in the Himalayan region. Its leaves are eaten as a vegetable during the summer months, a wild green that nourishes the mountain communities. Like many wild foods, it's a reminder of the abundance that grows in remote places.
identification: A herbaceous plant with divided leaves. The leaves are the primary edible portion.
fun_facts: Found in the Himalayas. Used as a vegetable. Harvested in August-September. Belongs to the Apiaceae family.
trivia: This species is one of the many lesser-known wild vegetables in the Himalayas that are used by local communities during the summer months. It's a part of the rich tradition of wild food gathering.

description: A climbing plant with unique, lantern-shaped flowers that trap insects. Its tubers are edible and are used as food and medicine. In Nepal, it's a lesser-known species, but in some parts of Asia, similar plants are valued for their medicinal properties.
identification: A climbing plant with fleshy stems and unique, tubular flowers. The tubers are the primary edible portion.
habitat: Grows in tropical and subtropical regions. Found in forests and along roadsides.
fun_facts: Found in tropical regions. Used in traditional medicine. Has unique flowers. Found in forests and roadsides.
trivia: The flowers of Ceropegia species are known for their unique, lantern-like shape and unusual pollination mechanism that involves trapping insects. The tubers of some species are used as food. In Nepal, it's a wild plant with edible tubers.

description: A medicinal shrub whose leaves and flowers are edible, but whose real value is in its bark—a traditional remedy for diarrhea and dysentery. In Ayurveda, it's known as kurchi and has been trusted for centuries. In Nepal, it grows wild in forest margins, a healer waiting to be found.
identification: A shrub or small tree reaching 3–5 m with opposite, oblong leaves and white flowers. The leaves and flowers are the edible portions.
habitat: Grows in tropical and subtropical regions. Found in forests and along roadsides.
fun_facts: Grows 3–5 m tall. Used in traditional medicine. Has medicinal properties. Harvested in May-June.
trivia: This plant is known in Ayurvedic medicine as 'Kurchi' and has been used for centuries as a remedy for diarrhea and dysentery. The seeds are also used for their medicinal properties. In Nepal, it's a valuable medicinal plant.

description: A toxic plant with a striking ornamental spathe—its flowers are a work of art, but its leaves are not to be eaten lightly. In some places, it's grown in gardens for its beauty, but the knowledge of its edibility is fading. In Nepal, it's a plant that sits between the wild and the cultivated.
identification: A herbaceous plant with a distinctive hooded flower spathe. The leaves are the edible portion after careful processing.
habitat: Grows in temperate and alpine regions. Found in forests and shady areas.
fun_facts: Found in the Himalayas. Toxic due to calcium oxalate. Known for its ornamental spathe. Found in forests.
trivia: The spathe (hooded flower) of this plant is a striking feature, often used as an ornamental in gardens. The plant is toxic when fresh due to calcium oxalate crystals. In Nepal, it's sometimes planted for its decorative value.

description: A plant whose toxic corms were once a food of last resort—carefully processed to remove the irritating crystals. In times of scarcity, the mountain communities knew how to make it safe. Today, it's a reminder of the hard times and the knowledge that sustained people through them.
identification: A herbaceous plant with a distinctive hooded flower spathe. The corms are the edible portion after processing.
habitat: Grows in temperate and alpine regions, often in moist, shady places.
fun_facts: Found in the Himalayas. Toxic due to calcium oxalate. Harvested in summer-rainy season. Used as food in times of scarcity.
trivia: The processing of Arisaema corms involves soaking, boiling, and changing the water multiple times to remove toxins. This knowledge is part of the traditional food culture of the hills. In Nepal, it's a survival food.

description: A high-altitude Arisaema found in dry areas. Its shoots are sometimes eaten after processing. It's a resilient plant that grows in harsh conditions, a symbol of the hardiness of mountain flora.
identification: A herbaceous plant with a small, hooded flower. The shoots are the edible portion after processing.
fun_facts: Found in the Himalayas. Toxic. Grows in dry areas.
trivia: Like other Arisaema species, it requires careful preparation. Its ability to grow in dry conditions makes it unique among the genus.

description: A Himalayan Arisaema whose shoots and leaves are sometimes gathered. The plant is toxic and requires processing, but it's a part of the wild food repertoire of the region.
identification: Similar to other Arisaema species.
fun_facts: Found in the Himalayas. Toxic. Shoots and leaves edible after processing.
trivia: The genus Arisaema is known for its unique and often bizarre inflorescences, which range from small to spectacular.

description: A plant with medicinal properties—its tubers are used in traditional medicine for their anticancer potential. However, they are toxic and require careful processing. In Nepal, it's known to healers.
identification: Similar to other Arisaema species.
fun_facts: Has anticancer properties. Toxic. Used in traditional medicine.
trivia: Arisaema jacquemontii is named after the French botanist Victor Jacquemont, who explored the Himalayas in the early 19th century.

description: A large Arisaema with a striking appearance—its spadix is long and snake-like. The plant is used in traditional medicine for colds and cough, but its tubers are toxic. In Nepal, it's a plant of both healing and danger.
identification: A large plant with a distinctive spathe and long, snake-like spadix.
fun_facts: Used for cold and cough. Has insecticidal properties. Toxic.
trivia: Arisaema tortuosum is one of the more commonly encountered species in the Himalayas. Its striking appearance makes it a favorite among plant enthusiasts.

description: Another high-altitude Arisaema, found in the Himalayas. Its shoots are edible after careful processing. It's a plant that tests the skill of the forager.
identification: Similar to other Arisaema species.
fun_facts: Found in the Himalayas. Toxic.
trivia: The processing of this plant's shoots is a skill that is passed down in mountain communities, ensuring safe consumption.

description: A taro relative, whose leaves are used as a vegetable. The plant contains calcium oxalate crystals, so it must be cooked thoroughly. In Nepal, karkalo leaves are a common green, often cooked in curries.
identification: A herbaceous plant with large, heart-shaped leaves. The leaves are the edible portion.
fun_facts: Leaves are edible after cooking. Contains calcium oxalate. Used as a vegetable.
trivia: This plant is closely related to the taro (Colocasia esculenta). In Nepal, it's often grown in home gardens for its leaves.

description: A wild taro species, found in moist, shaded areas. Its leaves and corms are edible after cooking. It's a lesser-known food source, but still used in times of need.
identification: Similar to cultivated taro.
fun_facts: Wild relative of taro. Edible after cooking.
trivia: Like cultivated taro, it contains calcium oxalate crystals that are destroyed by cooking.

description: A plant with edible shoots and medicinal uses. Its juice is used to relieve itch, and in traditional medicine, it's considered alexipharmic (an antidote). In Nepal, it's found in the Himalayas.
identification: A plant with heart-shaped leaves and above-ground bulbils.
fun_facts: Used to relieve itch. Has alexipharmic properties.
trivia: The plant produces bulbils that can sprout into new plants, aiding its spread.

description: A toxic plant in the arum family, with corms that can be eaten after careful processing. It's found in the Himalayas and is used as a famine food.
identification: A plant with a distinctive spathe and spotted petiole.
fun_facts: Toxic when fresh. Corms edible after processing.
trivia: The genus Sauromatum is known for its ability to produce heat to attract pollinators.

description: A tree whose young leaves are used as a vegetable. It's found in the Himalayas and is related to the ginseng family. The leaves are likely cooked as a green.
identification: A tree with compound leaves.
fun_facts: Young leaves edible. Related to ginseng.
trivia: Aralia species are known for their medicinal properties, similar to ginseng.

description: A tree whose young shoots are eaten as a vegetable. It's related to ginseng and found in the Himalayas. The shoots are probably cooked before eating.
identification: A tree with large, compound leaves.
fun_facts: Young shoots edible. Related to ginseng.
trivia: Macropanax species are less known than other araliaceae but provide food and medicine in their native ranges.

description: A dwarf palm with edible fruits and stems. In Nepal, its leaves are used for making mats and brooms. The fruits are edible and aperient.
identification: A small palm with a short trunk and feathery leaves.
fun_facts: Fruits edible. Used for mats and brooms.
trivia: This is a wild date palm, related to the cultivated date palm. Its fruits are smaller but similar in taste.

description: Another wild date palm, with edible fruits and leaves used for weaving. Found in Nepal, it provides both food and material for local communities.
identification: A palm with a short trunk and stiff leaves.
fun_facts: Fruits edible. Leaves used for weaving.
trivia: This palm is known for its spiky leaves, which are used to make brooms and baskets.

description: A palm with edible pith and fruits. However, its fruits can cause dermatitis. In Nepal, it's found in the Himalayas.
identification: A palm with a short trunk and large, feathery leaves.
fun_facts: Pith and fruits edible. May cause dermatitis.
trivia: This palm is interesting because its leaves are arranged in two rows along the stem, giving it a distichous appearance.

description: A wild asparagus found in Nepal. Its young shoots are eaten as a vegetable, similar to cultivated asparagus. It's a popular wild green in the hills.
identification: A climbing plant with feathery leaves and thorny stems. The young shoots are the edible portion.
fun_facts: Young shoots edible. Used as a tonic.
trivia: Wild asparagus is more slender than the cultivated variety but has a similar flavor. In Nepal, it's called 'ban kurilo.'

description: A plant with edible leaves, related to the spider plant. Found in Nepal, its leaves are used as a vegetable. It's a lesser-known wild green.
identification: A herbaceous plant with long, narrow leaves.
fun_facts: Leaves edible. Related to spider plant.
trivia: Chlorophytum species are often grown as ornamentals, but some are used as food in their native regions.

description: A plant with edible leaves and shoots, found in the Himalayas. It's related to the lily family and used as a vegetable.
identification: A herbaceous plant with oval leaves and small white flowers.
fun_facts: Leaves and shoots edible.
trivia: Maianthemum species are often called 'false Solomon's seals' and are valued for their edible shoots.

description: A plant with edible leaves, but caution—it may be poisonous to some. In Nepal, it's known to have diuretic properties and is sometimes used in traditional medicine, but not widely eaten.
identification: A herbaceous plant with whorled leaves.
fun_facts: Leaves edible with caution. Has diuretic properties.
trivia: This plant is considered potentially poisonous by some hill communities, so it's not commonly eaten.

description: A plant whose shoots are used in traditional medicine for joint pain and inflammation. In Nepal, it's not commonly eaten but valued for its medicinal properties.
identification: A herbaceous plant with fleshy stems and distinctive, spurred flowers.
fun_facts: Used for joint pain and inflammation. Leaf paste applied.
trivia: Impatiens species are often known as 'touch-me-nots' due to their explosive seed dispersal.

description: A tree whose fruits, pods, and flowers are used in traditional medicine. In Nepal, it's known for its use in cardiac disorders and as an ingredient in Chyawanprash. The pods are also sometimes used as a vegetable.
identification: A medium-sized tree with large, compound leaves and large, flat pods.
fun_facts: Used in traditional medicine. Pods are eaten. Part of Chyawanprash.
trivia: Oroxylum indicum is also called the 'tree of life' in some traditions. Its large pods are distinctive and are used as a vegetable in some parts of India.

description: A plant with edible leaves, found in the Himalayas. It's related to mustard and used as a vegetable. Its leaves have a peppery flavor.
identification: A herbaceous plant with pinnate leaves.
fun_facts: Leaves edible. Peppery flavor.
trivia: Cardamine species are known for their peppery taste, similar to watercress.

description: A plant with edible leaves, used as a vegetable in the Himalayas. Its leaves are a common wild green during early spring.
identification: Similar to other Cardamine species.
fun_facts: Leaves edible. Used as a green vegetable.
trivia: This plant is one of many wild mustards that provide early spring greens in the mountains.

description: A wild mustard with edible leaves and seeds. The leaves are used as a vegetable, and the seeds are likely used as a spice. It's found in the Himalayas.
identification: A herbaceous plant with narrow leaves and yellow flowers.
fun_facts: Leaves and seeds edible. Used as a spice.
trivia: Erysimum species are often called 'wallflowers' and are known for their fragrant flowers.

description: A plant with edible leaves, found in the Himalayas. It's used as a vegetable and is believed to have medicinal properties, including treating fever.
identification: A large herb with divided leaves.
fun_facts: Leaves edible. Used for fever. Found in the Himalayas.
trivia: This plant is part of the mustard family and may have a pungent taste.

description: A plant with edible leaves, used as a vegetable. It's a wild mustard with diuretic properties. Found in the Himalayas.
identification: A herb with pinnate leaves and yellow flowers.
habitat: Wet areas in tropical and subtropical regions.
fun_facts: Leaves edible. Has diuretic properties.
trivia: Rorippa species are often found in moist places and are related to watercress.

description: A plant whose roots are used as a tonic, similar to ginseng. In Nepal, it's used for cough, cold, and stomach disorders. Its roots are sometimes eaten as a vegetable.
identification: A climbing plant with bell-shaped flowers.
fun_facts: Roots used as a tonic. Used for cold and stomach issues.
trivia: Codonopsis is known as 'poor man's ginseng' and is used in traditional Chinese medicine for its adaptogenic properties.

description: A plant with edible fruits, related to the caper. Found in the tropics, its fruits are used as a vegetable. In Nepal, it's less known but part of local plant diversity.
identification: A shrub with thorny branches and edible fruits.
fun_facts: Fruits edible. Related to caper.
trivia: This plant is sometimes used as a substitute for caper in local cuisine.

description: A tree whose leaves are used as a vegetable. In traditional medicine, its bruised leaves are applied for rheumatism. Found in Nepal's tropical areas.
identification: A medium-sized tree with compound leaves and fragrant flowers.
fun_facts: Leaves used as a vegetable. Used for rheumatism.
trivia: The tree is also known as the 'garlic pear' because of the garlic-like aroma of its flowers.

description: Another Crateva species, its young leaves and shoots are used as a vegetable. Leaf juice is used for helminth infestation. Found in Nepal's tropical areas.
identification: Similar to C. religiosa.
fun_facts: Young leaves and shoots edible. Used for worms.
trivia: This plant is valued for its medicinal properties and is also used in traditional rituals.

description: A creeping herb with small, cordate leaves. Its leaves are used in traditional medicine for pain relief and wound healing. In Nepal, it's a common weed with medicinal uses.
identification: A creeping herb with small, heart-shaped leaves.
habitat: Moist, shady areas in tropical regions.
fun_facts: Used for pain and wound healing. Has anti-inflammatory effects.
trivia: Drymaria cordata is widely used in traditional medicine across Asia for its analgesic properties.

description: A subspecies of Drymaria cordata, with similar medicinal uses. It's used for fever, hepatoma, and malaria in traditional medicine.
identification: Similar to the parent species.
fun_facts: Used for fever and cancer. Has anti-inflammatory properties.
trivia: This plant is a valuable medicinal herb in many traditional systems, including Ayurveda and Chinese medicine.

description: A plant with edible leaves, found in the Himalayas. Its leaves are used as a vegetable. It's related to chickweed.
identification: Similar to chickweed.
fun_facts: Leaves edible. Found in the Himalayas.
trivia: Like chickweed, this plant is likely eaten as a mild green.

description: A plant with edible leaves and seeds. In traditional medicine, it's used for malarial fever, skin diseases, and leprosy. In Nepal, it's a lesser-known wild vegetable.
identification: An annual herb with compound leaves and yellow flowers.
habitat: Tropical and subtropical regions, in disturbed areas.
fun_facts: Leaves and seeds edible. Used for fever and skin diseases.
trivia: Cleome species are known for their pungent odor and are used in traditional medicine across Asia.

description: A plant with edible leaves, found in the Himalayas. Its leaves are used as a vegetable. It's related to the fairy bells.
identification: A herbaceous plant with oval leaves and small, bell-shaped flowers.
fun_facts: Leaves edible. Found in the Himalayas.
trivia: Disporum species are often grown as ornamentals for their delicate flowers.

description: A plant with edible roots and tubers, used as a vegetable. It's found in wet areas in the tropics. In Nepal, it's a lesser-known wild food.
identification: Similar to other dayflowers.
fun_facts: Roots and tubers edible. Found in wet areas.
trivia: The tubers of this plant are starchy and can be cooked like potatoes.

description: A plant whose shoots and leaves are used in fractured bones. In Nepal, its stem juice is used for sore eyes. It's a medicinal plant in the dayflower family.
identification: A creeping or climbing herb with blue flowers.
fun_facts: Used for fractures. Stem juice for sore eyes.
trivia: This plant is less known as a food but valued for its medicinal applications.

description: A plant with edible shoots, used as a vegetable during the rainy season. It's found in tropical regions.
identification: A creeping herb with small, blue flowers.
habitat: Moist, disturbed areas in the tropics.
fun_facts: Shoots edible. Used as a vegetable in rainy season.
trivia: Murdannia species are often used as green vegetables in Southeast Asia.

description: A plant whose flowers are used to relieve toothache. It's related to the toothache plant and has pesticidal properties. In Nepal, it's a medicinal plant.
identification: A herb with yellow, button-like flowers.
fun_facts: Flowers used for toothache. Has pesticidal properties.
trivia: Acmella oleracea, a related species, is known for its numbing effect on the tongue.

description: A plant with edible flowers, similar to the toothache plant. It's found in tropical regions.
identification: Similar to A. calva.
fun_facts: Flowers edible. Found in tropical regions.
trivia: Like other Acmella species, its flowers may have a tingling or numbing sensation when chewed.

description: A plant whose shoots are used for nausea, fever, and asthma. It's a medicinal plant in the aster family. Found in Nepal.
identification: A herb with toothed leaves and yellow flowers.
fun_facts: Used for nausea and fever. Found in Nepal.
trivia: Bidens species are known for their barbed seeds that cling to clothing and fur.

description: A plant whose leaves are used as a vegetable and in traditional medicine. Its juice is used for threadworm infections. In Nepal, it's a medicinal weed.
identification: A herb with hairy, toothed leaves and yellow flowers.
fun_facts: Leaves edible. Juice used for worms.
trivia: Blumea species are known for their aromatic properties and are used in traditional medicine for various ailments.

description: A thistle with edible shoots, found in the Himalayas. Its young shoots are used as a vegetable.
identification: A thistle with spiny leaves and purple flowers.
fun_facts: Shoots edible. Found in the Himalayas.
trivia: This thistle is named after the Danish botanist Nathaniel Wallich.

description: A plant whose leaves are used as a vegetable. Its decoction is used for fever and bowel complaints. In Nepal, it's a medicinal herb.
identification: A herb with reddish-purple stems and small, orange-red flowers.
habitat: Tropical and subtropical regions, in disturbed areas.
fun_facts: Leaves edible. Used for fever and bowel issues.
trivia: Emilia sonchifolia is also known as 'red tassel flower' and is used in traditional medicine in many parts of Asia.

description: A plant whose leaves are used as a vegetable. It's found in tropical regions. In Nepal, it's a lesser-known wild green.
identification: A herb with lobed leaves and yellow flowers.
fun_facts: Leaves edible. Found in tropical regions.
trivia: Launaea species are often used as greens in Africa and Asia.

description: A plant with edible leaves, used as a vegetable. It's a species of sow thistle found in Nepal.
identification: Similar to other sow thistles.
fun_facts: Leaves edible. Used in earache.
trivia: This sow thistle is likely used in a similar way to other Sonchus species.

description: A dandelion species from the Himalayas, whose leaves and flowers are used as a vegetable. It's used as a galactagogue.
identification: A rosette-forming herb with yellow flowers, similar to common dandelion.
fun_facts: Leaves and flowers edible. Used as a galactagogue.
trivia: Dandelion leaves are known for their bitter taste and are often used in salads and teas. This Himalayan species is used similarly.

description: Another Himalayan dandelion, with edible leaves and flowers. Used for bile and stomach disorders.
identification: Similar to other dandelions.
fun_facts: Leaves and flowers edible. Used for stomach and bile issues.
trivia: Like other dandelions, this plant is a nutritious wild green with medicinal properties.

description: A plant whose roots and shoots are used as a vegetable. It's a wild salsify found in the Himalayas.
identification: A herb with grass-like leaves and purple flowers.
fun_facts: Roots and shoots edible. Found in the Himalayas.
trivia: Salsify is known for its oyster-like flavor when cooked. This wild relative is used similarly.

description: A plant whose leaves and stems are used as a vegetable. Used for arthritis and diabetes.
identification: A succulent herb with fleshy leaves and small, pink flowers.
fun_facts: Leaves and stems edible. Used for arthritis.
trivia: This plant is similar to purslane and is used as a vegetable in some regions.

description: A shrub whose leaves are used as a vegetable. Used for dermatitis and boils.
identification: A shrub with large, toothed leaves.
fun_facts: Leaves edible. Used for dermatitis.
trivia: This nettle relative is used as a vegetable and in traditional medicine.

description: A plant whose leaves are used as a vegetable, found in the Himalayas.
identification: A herb with large, ovate leaves.
fun_facts: Leaves edible.
trivia: Elatostema species are often used as greens in the Himalayas.

description: A plant whose leaves are used as a vegetable. Poultice of leaves is used for abdominal disorders.
identification: Similar to E. platyphyllum.
fun_facts: Leaves edible. Used for abdominal disorders.
trivia: This plant is part of the nettle family but without stinging hairs.

description: A stinging nettle relative whose leaves are used as a vegetable. Its juice is applied for headache and joint pains. In Nepal, it's called allo.
identification: A tall herb with stinging hairs, large, toothed leaves.
fun_facts: Leaves edible. Used for headache. Stinging nettle relative.
trivia: This plant is used for fiber production and as a leafy vegetable.

description: A stinging nettle whose leaves are used as a vegetable. Used for fevers and joint pain.
identification: Similar to G. diversifolia.
fun_facts: Leaves edible. Used for fevers.
trivia: This plant is used in traditional medicine for its anti-inflammatory properties.

description: A plant whose leaves are used as a vegetable, found in the Himalayas.
identification: A herb with ovate leaves.
fun_facts: Leaves edible. Found in the Himalayas.
trivia: This plant is used locally as a green vegetable.

description: A shrub whose leaves are used as a vegetable. Used for pain, inflammation, and menstrual issues.
identification: A shrub with serrated leaves.
fun_facts: Leaves edible. Used for pain and inflammation.
trivia: This plant is also used for making ropes and cloths.

description: A plant whose leaves are used as a vegetable, found in the Himalayas.
identification: A herb with translucent leaves.
fun_facts: Leaves edible.
trivia: Pilea species are often used as leafy vegetables.

description: A plant with edible leaves, found in the Himalayas.
identification: Similar to other Pilea.
fun_facts: Leaves edible.
trivia: This plant grows in shaded, moist places.

description: A plant whose leaves are used as a vegetable. Used for pulmonary diseases and urinary infections.
identification: A herb with ovate leaves.
fun_facts: Leaves edible. Used for urinary infections.
trivia: This plant is a common weed and is used as a leafy green.

description: A high-altitude nettle whose shoots are used as a vegetable. Used for swelling and stomach cleaning.
identification: Similar to U. dioica.
fun_facts: Shoots edible. Used for swelling.
trivia: This nettle grows at extreme altitudes and is a valuable food resource.

description: A nettle whose leaves and inflorescence are used as a vegetable. Used as an expectorant and blood purifier.
identification: Similar to other nettles.
fun_facts: Leaves and inflorescence edible. Used as expectorant.
trivia: This nettle is used in traditional medicine for respiratory issues.

description: A climbing plant whose leaves are used as a vegetable. Used for kidney stones.
identification: A climbing vine with tendrils and fleshy leaves.
fun_facts: Leaves edible. Used for kidney stones.
trivia: Cissus species are related to grapes and are used in traditional medicine.

description: A plant whose stems are used as a vegetable, related to ginger. Found in the Himalayas.
identification: A herb with ginger-like stems and leaves.
fun_facts: Stems edible. Related to ginger.
trivia: Cautleya species are used like ginger in local cuisine.

One of the most commonly consumed ferns in Nepal, masinoniuro graces dinner tables across the country. The young fronds are gathered from the wild and cooked into a nutritious, iron-rich vegetable. In eastern Nepal, grandmothers will tell you to drink the cooking water—they say it's a gentle tonic for the stomach, a wisdom passed down through generations.
identification: A large fern with bright green, divided fronds growing up to 1.5 m long. The young, curled fronds (fiddleheads) are the edible portion. The plant has a short, creeping rhizome.
habitat: Grows in tropical and subtropical forests, often in moist, shaded areas along streams, roadsides, and forest edges at elevations from 100–1,300 m.
fun_facts: Fronds can grow up to 1.5 m long. Rich in iron, phosphorus, and potassium. One of the most popular wild vegetables in Nepal. In Southeast Asia, this fern is a common vegetable in markets.
trivia: In Nepal, the cooking water from this fern is often consumed as a gentle digestive remedy. The fern is so popular that it's commonly sold in local markets during the growing season. In Thailand, it's known as 'phak khut' and used in soups.

description: A fast-growing tree with edible flowers that resemble hummingbirds. In Nepal, the flowers are used as a vegetable, often cooked in curries or stir-fries. The plant also fixes nitrogen in the soil.
identification: A small, fast-growing tree reaching 5–10 m with compound leaves and large, white or red flowers that hang like bunches.
habitat: Grows in tropical and subtropical areas, often along roadsides and in gardens.
fun_facts: Grows 5–10 m tall. Flowers are edible. Used as a vegetable. Fixes nitrogen.
trivia: In Nepal, agasice flowers are a popular seasonal vegetable. The tree is also used for fodder and green manure. Its wood is light and used for making floats.

description: A climbing plant with itchy pods. Its fruits are edible but can cause itching. In Nepal, it's called kauso and is used for Parkinson's disease in traditional medicine.
identification: A vigorous climber with hairy pods that cause itching, and purple flowers.
fun_facts: Fruits edible with caution. Causes itching. Used for Parkinson's.
trivia: Velvet bean is a source of L-DOPA, a drug used to treat Parkinson's disease. The itching is due to serotonin-containing hairs.

fruit_type: Drupe (with a hard shell containing edible seed)
culinary_uses: Fresh or dried nuts; in baking and desserts
medicinal_uses: Rich in omega-3 fatty acids; good for brain health
cultural_significance: Used in festivals and religious ceremonies
economic_importance: Important cash crop in the high hills
description: The king of nuts—walnut (okhar) is a prized nut that grows in Nepal's high hills. The hard shell contains a brain-shaped kernel that's rich in healthy fats and nutrients. It's a valuable cash crop for hill farmers.
fun_facts: Walnuts are one of the oldest tree foods, with cultivation dating back to 7,000 BC.
They are rich in omega-3 fatty acids.
The shells are used for making dyes.
trivia: In Nepal, walnuts are often eaten during festivals and as a snack.

description: An aquatic herb that grows along streams, its hollow stems and mild celery flavor making it a favorite in stir-fries and soups. In Japan, it's called seri and is one of the seven spring herbs used in a traditional dish. In Nepal, it's known as nakuri, a wild green gathered from water edges.
identification: A perennial aquatic herb with hollow stems and divided leaves. The leaves and stems are the edible portions.
habitat: Grows in shallow water, along stream banks, and in wet areas. Found in Asia.
fun_facts: Found in Asia. Used for hepatitis. Has a mild celery flavor. Harvested in May-June.
trivia: This plant is closely related to the water hemlock, but it's safe to eat. In Japan, it's known as 'seri' and is one of the seven spring herbs used in a traditional rice dish. In Nepal, it's a common wild vegetable.

description: An aquatic plant that is a troublesome weed, but its leaves are used for burns and injuries. In Nepal, it's called jalkumbhi.
identification: A free-floating aquatic plant with thick, glossy leaves and showy purple flowers.
habitat: Tropical and subtropical regions, in freshwater bodies.
fun_facts: Used for burns. Considered a noxious weed. Can be used for fuel.
trivia: Water hyacinth is one of the most invasive weeds in the world, but it has uses in phytoremediation and as a biofuel.

description: An aquatic plant that forms floating rosettes on water surfaces. It's used as a green manure and as a food source for fish, and in some places, the leaves are eaten after cooking. It's also used in traditional medicine for its antiseptic properties.
identification: A free-floating aquatic plant with rosettes of soft, velvety leaves.
habitat: Grows in still freshwater bodies in tropical regions.
fun_facts: Provides food for fish. Used as green manure. Has antiseptic properties.
trivia: Water lettuce is a common aquatic weed in many parts of the world. In Nepal, it's found in ponds and lakes.

description: An aquatic plant whose shoots and leaves are a popular vegetable in many Asian cuisines. In Nepal, it's called karmi sag and is grown in wetlands. It's used in traditional medicine for piles and sleeplessness.
identification: A semi-aquatic vine with hollow stems and arrowhead-shaped leaves.
habitat: Grows in waterlogged areas, ditches, and rice paddies.
fun_facts: Shoots and leaves edible. Used in traditional medicine. Popular in Asian cuisine.
trivia: Water spinach is a common vegetable in Southeast Asia, often stir-fried or used in soups. It's highly nutritious and grows rapidly.

description: This aquatic fern thrives in rice paddies across Southeast Asia, where farmers gather it as a vegetable and green manure. Its young leaves, before they unfurl, are a market staple in Thailand and Vietnam. In Nepal, it's less commonly eaten, but its presence in watery fields connects it to a long tradition of wetland foraging.
identification: An aquatic fern with bright green, finely divided fronds growing in rosettes. The plant can be submerged or floating. The young leaves are the edible portion.
habitat: Grows in shallow water, ponds, ditches, and rice paddies. Found in tropical and subtropical regions worldwide.
fun_facts: Grows in shallow water. Found in tropical and subtropical regions worldwide. Used as a green manure in rice fields. Popular vegetable in South-East Asia.
trivia: This fern is so popular as a vegetable in Thailand that it's cultivated in rice paddies and sold in markets throughout the country. It's known locally as 'phak koot.' In Nepal, it's sometimes found in similar wetland habitats.

description: An aquatic plant with peppery leaves, watercress is a well-known edible green. In Nepal, it grows in streams and is used as a vegetable. It's rich in vitamins and has anti-inflammatory properties.
identification: A floating or creeping aquatic plant with small, round leaves and white flowers.
habitat: Grows in shallow, flowing water in temperate regions.
fun_facts: Leaves edible and peppery. Rich in vitamins. Used in salads.
trivia: Watercress is considered one of the oldest known leaf vegetables consumed by humans. It's a popular ingredient in sandwiches and salads.

culinary_uses: Fresh, in juice
medicinal_uses: Rich in vitamin C and antioxidants
description: The quintessential summer fruit—watermelon (kharbuja) is a refreshing, juicy fruit that's a favorite in Nepal's Terai. The sweet, red flesh is a welcome relief from the summer heat.
fun_facts: Watermelon is 92% water.
It's rich in vitamin C and antioxidants.
The fruit is native to Africa.
trivia: In Nepal, watermelon is often eaten during the hot summer months.

description: A plant whose leaves and shoots are used as a vegetable. Used to cure ulcers.
identification: A semi-aquatic herb with fleshy stems and small, white flowers.
fun_facts: Leaves and shoots edible. Used for ulcers.
trivia: This plant is a common weed in rice fields and is sometimes used as a vegetable.

leaf_shape: Flat, narrow, with auricles at base
culinary_uses: Ground into flour for roti, chapati, bread, noodles
medicinal_uses: Wheat bran for digestive health
economic_importance: Second most important cereal; covers ~20% of cropped area
description: The silent hero of the Nepali kitchen—wheat is what turns into the daily roti and chapati that keep us going. While rice gets all the glory, wheat quietly covers the second-largest area of any crop in Nepal.
fun_facts: Wheat covers about 20% of Nepal's total cropped area.
Nepal produces around 2 million metric tons of wheat annually.
The crop is vital for the winter season, providing flour for the famous Gwaramari bread of the Newar community.
trivia: Wheat was first domesticated in the Fertile Crescent over 10,000 years ago. In Nepal, the spring wheat harvest is a busy time, with families threshing the grain on open courtyards.

uses: Rootstocks for commercial apple sapling production
description: The wild apple is the ancestor of the cultivated apple—it's small, tart, and often bitter. In Nepal, it's valued not for its fruit but as a rootstock for grafting apple varieties. Its hardy root system gives cultivated trees resistance to diseases and harsh conditions. It's the hidden foundation of Nepal's apple industry.
identification: A medium-sized deciduous tree reaching 8–12 m with oval, serrated leaves. The fruit is small, 1–2 cm in diameter, round, red or yellow, with sour flesh.
habitat: Grows in temperate forests at elevations of 1,000–2,500 m. Found in the mid- to high-hills.
fun_facts: Grows 8–12 m tall. Fruits are 1–2 cm in diameter. Used as a rootstock. Hardy and disease-resistant. The ancestor of cultivated apples.
trivia: In Nepal, wild apple rootstocks are collected from the forests and used in commercial orchards. The fruit itself is sometimes made into jelly or cider. In its native range, it's an important food for wildlife.

description: A wild relative of the apricot, found in Nepal's mid-hills. Its fruits are smaller and more tart than cultivated apricots, but they are sometimes gathered for local use. The tree is also valued for its wood and as a genetic resource.
identification: A deciduous tree reaching 5–10 m with oval, serrated leaves. The fruit is small, 2–3 cm in diameter, round, yellow-orange, with a sour taste.
habitat: Grows in temperate forests in the mid-hills.
fun_facts: Grows 5–10 m tall. Fruits are 2–3 cm in diameter. Related to cultivated apricot. Found in the mid-hills.
trivia: In Nepal, the wild apricot is sometimes used for making jams or pickles. The tree is also a source of timber and firewood. It's an important resource for forest-dwelling communities.

description: A wild banana native to Nepal, found in the mid-hills. Unlike the cultivated banana, its fruits are small and full of seeds. It's more used as a source of fiber and as an ornamental, though the seeds are sometimes eaten after cooking.
identification: A large herbaceous plant with a pseudostem and large, paddle-shaped leaves. The fruit is a small, seeded banana, 5–10 cm long.
habitat: Grows in moist, shady areas in the mid-hills at 1,400–1,650 m.
fun_facts: A large herb. Fruits are small and seeded. Found in Nepal. Related to the cultivated banana.
trivia: In Nepal, this wild banana is sometimes grown for its ornamental value. The seeds are hard and not usually consumed, but the plant's fibers are used for weaving.

description: A wild relative of caraway, growing in the meadows of Nepal's high hills. Its leaves are edible, and its seeds are used as a spice—a tradition that stretches back to ancient Egypt, where caraway was cultivated in the Nile Valley. In Nepal, it's a lesser-known herb, but its flavor is distinctive.
identification: A biennial herb reaching 0.5–1 m with feathery leaves and small, brown seeds. The leaves are the primary edible portion.
habitat: Grows in temperate regions of Asia and Europe. Found in meadows and grasslands.
fun_facts: Grows 0.5–1 m tall. Used as a spice. Found in Asia and Europe. Used in traditional medicine.
trivia: Caraway is one of the oldest cultivated spices, with evidence of its use dating back to ancient Egypt. The wild variety in Nepal is known for its distinct flavor and medicinal properties. In Europe, caraway is used in rye bread and cheeses.

description: A wild relative of the kiwifruit, found in Nepal's forests. Its small, edible fruits are similar to the cultivated kiwi but much smaller and hairier. It's a species that could be a source of genetic diversity for breeding, but for now, it remains a curiosity for foragers.
identification: A climbing vine with hairy stems and large, heart-shaped leaves. The fruit is small, 2–4 cm long, brown and hairy, with green, seedy flesh.
habitat: Grows in temperate forests, often climbing on trees and shrubs.
fun_facts: A climbing vine. Fruits are 2–4 cm long. Related to cultivated kiwi. Found in the wild.
trivia: In Nepal, wild kiwifruit is sometimes gathered and eaten fresh, though it's less sweet than the commercial varieties. The plant is also used in traditional medicine.

description: The wild mango is smaller and more fibrous than its cultivated cousin, but its flavor is just as intense. Found in the forests of Nepal's mid-hills, it is sometimes used as an appetizer—its sourness stimulates the appetite. It's a reminder of the diversity hidden in the wild, waiting to be discovered.
identification: A small to medium-sized deciduous tree reaching 10–15 m with bushy growth. The fruit is oval, 5–8 cm long, with greenish-yellow skin and fibrous, sour flesh.
habitat: Grows in tropical and subtropical forests in the mid-hills. Prefers well-drained soil and full sun.
fun_facts: Grows 10–15 m tall. Fruits are 5–8 cm long. Flowering occurs in February-April. Used as an appetizer. Related to the cultivated mango.
trivia: Wild mangoes are often harvested by forest dwellers and used in traditional dishes. In some regions, they are considered a famine food. The wood is also used for furniture.

description: A wild species of olive found in Nepal. Its fruits are smaller and less oily than cultivated olives, but they are sometimes harvested for their oil or used as a condiment. It's a hardy plant that grows in dry, rocky areas.
identification: A small evergreen tree reaching 5–10 m with leathery, lance-shaped leaves. The fruit is a small drupe, 1–2 cm long, green to black when ripe.
habitat: Grows in dry, rocky areas in subtropical and temperate zones.
fun_facts: Grows 5–10 m tall. Fruits are 1–2 cm long. Related to cultivated olive. Found in dry areas.
trivia: In some regions, the oil from this wild olive is extracted and used for cooking and skincare. The wood is also used for furniture and fuel.

description: Another wild olive species, similar to O. ferruginea, found in Nepal. Its fruits are also edible, and the tree shares similar uses. It contributes to the genetic diversity of the genus.
identification: A small evergreen tree with leathery leaves and small drupes.
habitat: Grows in similar habitats to O. ferruginea.
fun_facts: Related to O. ferruginea. Found in Nepal. Fruits edible.
trivia: Both species of wild olive are part of the rich flora of Nepal's lower mountain ranges.

description: Edimayal is a wild pear found in Nepal's mid-hills. Its fruits are small and gritty, but the tree is valuable as a rootstock for commercial pear varieties. It's a tough, adaptable tree that can grow in poor soils. The fruits are sometimes eaten by locals, but they are not as sweet as cultivated pears.
identification: A medium-sized deciduous tree reaching 8–15 m with oval, serrated leaves. The fruit is small, 2–4 cm in diameter, round to pear-shaped, with brownish-yellow skin and gritty flesh.
habitat: Grows in temperate forests at elevations of 1,000–2,500 m. Found in the mid-hills.
fun_facts: Grows 8–15 m tall. Fruits are 2–4 cm in diameter. Used as a rootstock. Gritty flesh. Found in the mid-hills.
trivia: In Nepal, the wild pear is often used as a rootstock for grafting. The fruits are occasionally made into preserves. The tree's wood is also used for fuel and tools.

description: Jangali aaru is an underutilized wild plum found across Nepal's temperate zones. Its fruits are edible but not widely commercialized, often gathered by locals for personal use. It's a species that holds potential for breeding and as a food source, but for now, it remains a forest treasure.
identification: A deciduous tree reaching 8–12 m with oval, serrated leaves. The fruit is small, 2–3 cm in diameter, round, purple-red when ripe, with a sweet-tart flesh.
habitat: Grows in temperate forests from eastern to western Nepal.
fun_facts: Grows 8–12 m tall. Fruits are 2–3 cm in diameter. Underutilized wild fruit. Found in temperate regions.
trivia: In Nepal, this plum is often eaten fresh or made into chutney. Its potential as a crop is being explored by researchers. The tree also provides habitat for wildlife.

description: A small, wild strawberry found in Nepal's mid-hills. Its fruits are smaller and less sweet than cultivated strawberries, but they are still a treat for foragers. It grows in shady, moist places and spreads by runners.
identification: A low-growing herb with trifoliate leaves and runners. The fruit is a small red berry, 0.5–1 cm in diameter, with seeds on the surface.
habitat: Grows in moist, shady areas in the mid-hills.
fun_facts: A low-growing herb. Fruits are small, 0.5–1 cm. Found in the mid-hills. Related to cultivated strawberry.
trivia: In Nepal, these wild strawberries are sometimes eaten fresh or used in jams. The plant is also used in traditional medicine for skin conditions.

origin_center: Various species from Africa, Asia, and Americas
culinary_uses: Boiled, fried, curried
medicinal_uses: Good source of carbohydrates and minerals
description: A climbing vine with large, starchy tubers. Yams are a traditional food in Nepal's hills and Terai, often eaten during festivals. The tubers can be quite large and are rich in carbohydrates.
fun_facts: Yams are not related to sweet potatoes.
Some yam tubers can grow to over 100 kg.
They are a staple food in many parts of Africa and Asia.
trivia: In Nepal, yam is often cooked with meat or as a vegetable curry.

description: A golden wild treasure of Nepal's hills—ainselu glows like sunshine in the forest. These sweet-tart berries are a cherished childhood memory for every hill Nepali. Children spend hours foraging for these golden gems during the summer months. While raspberries are grown commercially in many countries, Nepal's golden variety is a unique local treasure.
identification: A thorny, scrambling shrub or vine reaching 1–3 m. Leaves are oval with serrated edges and a yellow-green color. The fruit is small, 1–2 cm in diameter, bright yellow to golden-orange, soft, and covered in tiny segments.
habitat: Grows in temperate forests, forest edges, and open hillsides. Found throughout Nepal's mid-hills. Prefers well-drained soil and partial to full sun.
fun_facts: Grows 1–3 m tall. Fruits are 1–2 cm in diameter. Rich in vitamin C and antioxidants. A popular wild fruit in Nepal. Wild raspberries are found across Europe, North America, and Asia.
trivia: Ainselu is called the 'golden raspberry' for its bright color. In Nepal, children often spend hours foraging for these berries during summer. In Scotland, wild raspberries have been foraged for centuries.

description: A plant whose leaves are used as a vegetable. It may have narcotic effects, so caution is advised.
identification: A slender annual herb with tendrils and yellow flowers.
fun_facts: Leaves edible. May have narcotic effects.
trivia: Some Lathyrus species contain neurotoxins, so this plant is not widely eaten.
